With that infrastructure in place, Chang'e 4 became the first spacecraft to soft-land on the far side. The Yutu-2 rover has been operating since January 2019 and has driven ~1.6 km as of 2024, making it the longest-operating lunar rover in history.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Long March 3B from Xichang.

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Lander touches down at Von Kármán Crater 2019-01-03 — first spacecraft on the far side. All comms via Queqiao relay at Earth-Moon L2.

events.label: YUTU-2 DEPLOYED
events.note: Rover rolls down ramp.

missions/moon/change5.json.name: Chang'e 5
missions/moon/change5.json.first: First lunar sample return in 44 years (since Luna 24, 1976)
missions/moon/change5.json.description: Chang'e 5 was the first sample return from the Moon since the Soviet Union's Luna 24 in 1976 — a 44-year gap. The architecture: orbiter + lander + ascent vehicle + sample-return capsule, all in one launch. The lander touched down at Mons Rümker, drilled and scooped 1.731 kg of regolith, lifted off, rendezvoused and docked with the orbiter (the first robotic lunar rendezvous), and the capsule returned to Earth. The samples are from a region only 2 billion years old — much younger than any Apollo or Luna sample, rewriting models of lunar volcanism.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Long March 5 from Wenchang.

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Lander descends to Mons Rümker (Oceanus Procellarum) 2020-12-01.

events.label: SAMPLING
events.note: 1.731 kg collected via scoop and drill.

events.label: ASCENT
events.note: Ascent vehicle lifts off lunar surface.

events.label: RENDEZVOUS
events.note: First robotic lunar rendezvous; sample container transferred to orbiter.

events.label: EARTH RETURN
events.note: Sample capsule lands in Inner Mongolia 2020-12-16.

missions/moon/change6.json.name: Chang'e 6
missions/moon/change6.json.first: First sample return from the lunar far side
missions/moon/change6.json.description: Combines the architectures of Chang'e 4 (far-side communications) and Chang'e 5 (sample return). The Queqiao-2 relay satellite was launched first (March 2024) to support the mission. Chang'e 6 then collected 1.935 kg from Apollo Crater on the far side — material with very different composition from any lunar sample previously returned. The Moon's two hemispheres are radically different (the far side has thicker crust, fewer mare); these samples may finally explain why.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Long March 5 from Wenchang.

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Lander descends to Apollo Crater (far side) 2024-06-02. All comms via Queqiao-2 relay.

events.label: SAMPLING
events.note: 1.935 kg collected from far-side regolith.

events.label: ASCENT
events.note: Ascent vehicle lifts off; rendezvous with orbiter.

events.label: EARTH RETURN
events.note: Capsule lands in Inner Mongolia 2024-06-25 with the first far-side samples ever recovered.

missions/moon/clementine.json.name: Clementine
missions/moon/clementine.json.first: Joint NASA-DoD lunar mission; first hints of water ice at lunar poles
missions/moon/clementine.json.description: Designed primarily as a Strategic Defense Initiative technology demonstrator, Clementine spent 10 weeks in lunar orbit returning the first systematic global topographic and multispectral map of the Moon. Bistatic radar measurements at the lunar south pole produced the first tantalising hints of water ice — confirmed years later by Lunar Prospector and Chandrayaan-1. The follow-on mission to flyby the asteroid Geographos failed when a thruster malfunction depleted the spacecraft's propellant.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Titan II G from Vandenberg AFB.

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion 1994-02-19.

events.label: MAPPING BEGIN
events.note: Systematic multispectral and topographic mapping starts.

events.label: DEPARTURE
events.note: Departs lunar orbit for Geographos asteroid flyby.

events.label: THRUSTER FAIL
events.note: Onboard thruster malfunction depletes propellant; asteroid encounter cancelled.

missions/moon/lro.json.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
missions/moon/lro.json.description: Orbiting the Moon since 2009 at 50 km mean lunar altitude, LRO's narrow-angle camera images at 50 cm/pixel — high enough to see Apollo descent stages, rover tracks, and astronaut footpaths still preserved in the regolith. It found Lunokhod 1 thirty-nine years after the rover went dark. It identified 200+ candidate landing sites for Artemis. The water ice deposits at the lunar south pole that drive every modern lunar programme were quantified by LRO instruments. A scout mission that became the foundation of the modern lunar era.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 401 from Cape Canaveral SLC-41 (carried LCROSS impactor as secondary).

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion 2009-06-23.

events.label: PRIME MISSION
events.note: 1-year exploration phase (NASA programme) begins.

events.label: EXTENDED SCIENCE
events.note: Mission extended to multi-year science phase under NASA SMD.

missions/moon/luna10.json.name: Luna 10
missions/moon/luna10.json.first: First spacecraft to orbit the Moon (and any body other than Earth)
missions/moon/luna10.json.description: Launched 1966-03-31 from Baikonur, Luna 10 became the first spacecraft to orbit the Moon — and the first artificial satellite of any body other than Earth — when it inserted into a 350 × 1017 km lunar orbit at 71.9° inclination on 1966-04-03. Two and a half years before Apollo 8 reached the Moon with humans aboard. Carried a magnetometer, gamma-ray spectrometer, infrared radiometer, micrometeoroid detectors, plasma sensors, and a radio probe of the lunar gravity field. The gamma-ray data was the first compositional remote sensing of the Moon, suggesting basalt-like mare composition. Famously broadcast the Internationale anthem during the 23rd Congress of the Soviet Communist Party on 1966-04-04 — a propaganda flourish more than science. Operated 56 days / 460 orbits before its NiCd batteries depleted on 1966-05-30; remains in lunar orbit.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Molniya-M from Baikonur 1966-03-31 10:46 UTC.

events.label: TLI
events.note: Block-L upper stage propels Luna 10 toward Moon.

events.label: LOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion 1966-04-03 — first artificial satellite of any body other than Earth.

events.label: INTERNATIONALE BROADCAST
events.note: Broadcast the Internationale during the 23rd Congress of the Soviet Communist Party (1966-04-04).

events.label: EOL
events.note: NiCd batteries depleted; mission ended 1966-05-30. Remains in lunar orbit.

missions/moon/luna16.json.name: Luna 16
missions/moon/luna16.json.first: First robotic lunar sample return; first non-American lunar samples
missions/moon/luna16.json.description: Luna 16 was the Soviet Union's first successful robotic sample-return mission and the first non-crewed lunar return of any kind. After Apollo 11 brought home 22 kg of crewed samples in 1969, Luna 16 returned 101 grams of regolith from Mare Fecunditatis a year later — a fraction of Apollo's payload, but a profound proof-of-concept for the alternative architecture. The mission used a Proton-K booster and a direct return profile: descent to the surface, drill core, ascent stage launch, ballistic return capsule to Kazakhstan. The technique was reused for Luna 20 and Luna 24, and decades later by Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K from Baikonur 1970-09-12.

events.label: TLI
events.note: Trans-lunar injection on the Blok-D upper stage.

events.label: TCM
events.note: Mid-course correction during 4.5-day cruise.

events.label: LANDING
events.note: Soft landing in Mare Fecunditatis 1970-09-20. Surface ops + drill core (101 g).

events.label: SAMPLE RETURN
events.note: Capsule recovered in Kazakhstan 1970-09-24. First non-crewed lunar sample return.

missions/moon/luna17.json.name: Luna 17 / Lunokhod 1
missions/moon/luna17.json.first: First teleoperated rover to operate on another world
missions/moon/luna17.json.description: The first wheels on the Moon — driven from a control room in Crimea. Lunokhod 1 was a 322 kg pressurised tub mounted on eight independently-driven wheels, controlled by a five-person team in real time across the 2.5-second light-speed delay. It drove 10.5 km over 11 lunar days (322 Earth days), photographed 20,000+ scenes, and operated long past its 90-day design lifetime. Lost to history in the 1970s, located again in 2010 when NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted it sitting where it stopped.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K with Blok-D upper stage from Baikonur.

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion; orbital corrections to descent inclination.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Soft-landing at Mare Imbrium 1970-11-17.

events.label: ROVER DEPLOYED
events.note: Lunokhod 1 rolls down ramps onto lunar surface.

events.label: FINAL CONTACT
events.note: Last command session 1971-09-14; rover preserved in cold lunar night.

missions/moon/luna21.json.name: Luna 21 / Lunokhod 2
missions/moon/luna21.json.first: Second Soviet lunar rover; longest off-world drive (~39 km) for over 40 years
missions/moon/luna21.json.description: Luna 21 delivered Lunokhod 2, the Soviet Union's second crewed-controlled lunar rover, to Le Monnier crater on the southern edge of Mare Serenitatis in January 1973. The rover was driven from a control room in Crimea by a five-person team and traversed approximately 39 km over four lunar days — a record off-world distance that held until NASA's Opportunity rover passed it on Mars in 2014. Lunokhod 2 returned 80,000 television frames and 86 panoramas before dust contamination of its solar arrays ended operations.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K from Baikonur 1973-01-08.

events.label: TLI
events.note: Trans-lunar injection on the Blok-D upper stage.

events.label: TCM
events.note: Mid-course correction during cruise.

events.label: LANDING
events.note: Soft landing in Le Monnier crater 1973-01-15. Lunokhod 2 rolled off ramps a few hours later.

events.label: ROVER ACTIVE
events.note: Five-person ground crew in Crimea began driving operations. Total traverse: ~39 km.

missions/moon/luna24.json.name: Luna 24
missions/moon/luna24.json.first: Last Soviet lunar mission; last uncrewed lunar landing for 37 years
missions/moon/luna24.json.description: The Soviet Union's final lunar mission and the last uncrewed lunar landing until China's Chang'e 3 in 2013 — a gap of 37 years. The drilled core extracted regolith from 2 m depth and returned 170 g to Earth. A 1978 Soviet analysis reported ~0.1% water by mass in the core — an unconfirmed, still-debated result — foreshadowing later confirmed detections of lunar water. Luna 24 also marked the closure of the Soviet lunar programme; resources shifted to Mars and Venus.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K from Baikonur 1976-08-09.

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Soft-landing at Mare Crisium 1976-08-18.

events.label: DRILLING
events.note: Core sample extracted from 2 m depth.

events.label: ASCENT
events.note: Ascent stage lifts off; trans-Earth injection.

events.label: EARTH RETURN
events.note: Capsule lands in Surgut, USSR 1976-08-22 with 170 g of regolith.

missions/moon/luna9.json.name: Luna 9
missions/moon/luna9.json.first: First soft-landing on the Moon; first photographs from the lunar surface
missions/moon/luna9.json.description: After 11 Soviet failures and 5 American Ranger missions designed only to crash, Luna 9 became the first spacecraft to soft-land on another world. Nine images — including five panoramas — returned across three sessions over three days settled a long-running scientific debate: the Moon's surface was solid, not a sea of dust deep enough to swallow a lander. The mission lasted 3 days before battery depletion. Within months, every Moon-bound mission afterwards used soft-landing as the baseline.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Molniya-M from Baikonur 1966-01-31.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Soft-landing at Oceanus Procellarum 1966-02-03 18:45 UTC. First soft-landing on another world.

events.label: FIRST IMAGES
events.note: Nine images including five panoramas, returned in three transmission sessions over three days.

events.label: SIGNAL LOSS
events.note: Battery depleted; final transmission 1966-02-06.

missions/moon/lunar-prospector.json.name: Lunar Prospector
missions/moon/lunar-prospector.json.first: Neutron-spectrometer hydrogen finding at both lunar poles
missions/moon/lunar-prospector.json.description: The third NASA Discovery-class mission and the first NASA-managed dedicated lunar orbiter of the post-Apollo era. Launched 1998-01-07 on an Athena II from Cape Canaveral, Lunar Prospector entered a 100-km circular polar lunar orbit on 1998-01-11. The 296-kg spinning spacecraft carried five instruments: a gamma-ray spectrometer for global crustal composition, a neutron spectrometer for hydrogen / water-ice detection at the poles, an alpha-particle spectrometer for radon gas (indirect volcanism detection), a magnetometer + electron reflectometer for crustal magnetism, and a Doppler gravity experiment. Boynton-team analysis of the neutron data (Feldman et al., Science 281 + 284) found sharp neutron-flux deficits over both lunar poles — consistent with ~2 × 10⁹ tonnes of hydrogen-rich material (probably water ice) in permanently shadowed polar craters. Mission ended 1999-07-31 with deliberate impact near Shackleton crater hoping to release a detectable water-vapour plume; none was seen. The hydrogen finding stood until LCROSS and Chandrayaan-1 / M3 (2009) provided independent confirmation.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Athena II from Cape Canaveral SLC-46 1998-01-07 02:28 UTC.

events.label: TLI
events.note: Trans-lunar injection.

events.label: LOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion 1998-01-11 — initial 100 × 100 km polar orbit.

events.label: POLAR HYDROGEN
events.note: Neutron-spectrometer detects sharp neutron-flux deficits over both lunar poles — strong hydrogen signal, consistent with polar water ice.

events.label: SHACKLETON IMPACT
events.note: Deliberate impact near Shackleton crater 1999-07-31 09:52 UTC. No water-vapour plume detected from Earth.

missions/moon/slim.json.name: SLIM
missions/moon/slim.json.first: First precision landing within 100 m of target on another world
missions/moon/slim.json.description: Until SLIM, lunar landings had a kilometre-scale targeting accuracy. JAXA's Smart Lander demonstrated 100 m accuracy — the precision required for crewed missions to dock with pre-positioned cargo, for sample-return ascent vehicles to find their orbital partners, and for any future architecture that depends on landing at specific scientifically valuable sites. SLIM also pioneered low-energy ballistic transfer to the Moon, taking 135 days to arrive but using less propellant than direct trajectories. A demonstration of the patience interplanetary missions can afford when timeline isn't the binding constraint.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: H-IIA 202 from Tanegashima 2023-09-06.

events.label: BALLISTIC TRANSFER
events.note: Low-energy ballistic capture trajectory in progress.

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Soft-landing at Shioli Crater 2024-01-19 15:20 UTC. Within target accuracy: ~55 m off centre.

events.label: TILTED LANDING
events.note: Lander resting nose-down due to engine anomaly during final descent. Solar panels initially in shadow.

events.label: POWER RESUMED
events.note: Sun angle changes; solar panels generate power; operations resumed for one lunar day.

missions/moon/smart-1.json.name: SMART-1
missions/moon/smart-1.json.first: First European spacecraft to reach the Moon; first mission to reach the Moon under ion propulsion
missions/moon/smart-1.json.description: ESA's first lunar mission and the first European spacecraft to reach the Moon. SMART = Small Missions for Advanced Research in Technology — and the key technology was a Hall-effect solar-electric ion thruster (PPS-1350-G), at the time the largest such thruster ever flown. Launched 2003-09-27 as a shared payload on an Ariane 5 from Kourou, the 367-kg spacecraft used its 1.2-kW xenon ion drive over 13 months to slowly raise its Earth orbit, eventually captured by lunar gravity on 2004-11-15 — a 13-month low-thrust spiral rather than the days-long chemical transfer of every prior lunar mission. Operated for 16 months in a polar lunar orbit returning AMIE camera imagery, the first X-ray fluorescence elemental maps of the Moon (D-CIXS), and infrared mineral spectroscopy (SIR). Deliberately impacted Lacus Excellentiae (34.4° S, 46.2° W) on 2006-09-03 05:42 UTC — the impact flash was observed live from the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Ariane 5G from Kourou 2003-09-27 23:14 UTC — shared payload with Insat-3E + e-Bird.

events.label: ION DRIVE START
events.note: PPS-1350-G Hall-effect ion thruster begins 13-month low-thrust spiral.

events.label: LUNAR CAPTURE
events.note: Captured by lunar gravity 2004-11-15 — first European spacecraft at the Moon.

events.label: D-CIXS MAPPING
events.note: D-CIXS X-ray fluorescence delivers first global elemental maps of the Moon.

events.label: LACUS EXCELLENTIAE IMPACT
events.note: Deliberate impact at 34.4° S, 46.2° W on 2006-09-03 05:42 UTC. Impact flash observed from CFHT.

missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.name: Voyager 2
missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.first: Only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune; Grand Tour of four giant planets
missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.dispatch: Voyager 2 flew the tour that may never be flown again. Launched sixteen days before its twin on a slower, longer arc, it is the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune — two worlds that remain, decades later, known to us almost entirely from the few hours it spent racing past each one. It found a planet tipped on its side, the fastest winds in the solar system, and a frozen moon venting geysers into space, and then it too crossed into interstellar space, in 2018. Every serious plan to return to the ice giants still rests on what this single spacecraft saw on its way out.
missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.description: The twin that kept going when budgets tightened, Voyager 2 carried the Grand Tour from Jupiter and Saturn out to Uranus and Neptune — still the only close-up images we have of the ice giants. Its Neptune encounter in 1989 revealed the Great Dark Spot and Triton's geysers. Today both Voyagers sail in interstellar space with a golden record as humanity's calling card. Orrery lists Neptune as the catalogue destination; the real path relied on multiple gravity assists.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Titan IIIE lifts Voyager 2 from Cape Canaveral on a Grand-Tour trajectory.

events.label: NEPTUNE CLOSEST APPROACH
events.note: Flyby of Neptune and large moon Triton; last planetary encounter of the Grand Tour.

missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.name: New Horizons
missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.first: First flyby of Pluto and its moons; sharpest images of a Kuiper belt world
missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.dispatch: New Horizons had exactly one chance and took it. There was no orbit and no way to slow down — nine and a half years of travel, the fastest launch in history, all converging on a few hours at Pluto, executed by a machine so far away that each command took hours to arrive. It nailed the flyby on 14 July 2015 and overturned the expectation of a dead world: Pluto turned out to have mountains of water ice, a vast heart-shaped glacier of frozen nitrogen still slowly churning, and a young, active surface no one thought a body that small and cold could keep. Then it flew on to Arrokoth, a billion kilometres past Pluto — the most distant world ever seen up close — and it is still going.
missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.description: A nine-year sprint after the fastest launch to date, New Horizons compressed decades of anticipation into one July 2015 day — a world turned from a pixelated blur into mountains of water ice and nitrogen glaciers on Pluto's heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio. The spacecraft later flew Arrokoth, linking the mission to the primordial solar system. Flight arcs in Orrery are direct-transfer teaching models, not the actual Jupiter gravity assist.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 551 leaves Earth on a Jupiter-gravity-assist path to Pluto.

events.label: PLUTO FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach to Pluto; high-rate imaging and plasma data flood Earth.

missions/psyche/psyche-mission.json.name: Psyche
missions/psyche/psyche-mission.json.first: First mission to a metal-rich M-class asteroid; first use of Hall-effect ion thrusters as the primary cruise propulsion
missions/psyche/psyche-mission.json.description: Psyche reaches for the exposed nickel-iron core of a differentiated proto-planet — a 226-km metal body that may be the closest analogue to Earth's own core anywhere accessible. Launched 2023-10-13 on a Falcon Heavy from Kennedy LC-39A. Four SPT-140 Hall-effect ion thrusters spiral the trajectory outward; a Mars gravity assist in May 2026 (4,609 km closest approach) added the energy ion thrust alone couldn't deliver in time. Arrival planned 2029-08, followed by a 26-month four-orbit-phase descent (A → B → C → D) mapping the asteroid's gravity, magnetism, topography, and composition. If the metal-core hypothesis is right, Psyche will look unlike anything else we've visited — bare metal surface, iron-sulphide deposits, none of the rubble-pile chaos of typical asteroids.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Falcon Heavy from Kennedy LC-39A.

events.label: ION CRUISE BEGINS
events.note: Four Hall-effect ion thrusters take over. Continuous low-thrust acceleration over 4+ years.

events.label: MARS GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: 2026-05-15. Closest approach 4,609 km — Mars flyby completed.

events.label: PSYCHE ARRIVAL
events.note: Ion-thrust gravitational capture into 700-km orbit. 26-month mission, four orbit phases.

missions/saturn/cassini.json.name: Cassini-Huygens
missions/saturn/cassini.json.first: 13 years in orbit around Saturn — Huygens landed on Titan 2005-01-14 (first outer-solar-system soft landing)
missions/saturn/cassini.json.dispatch: Cassini did what no spacecraft had done at any giant planet: it stopped. For thirteen years it lived at Saturn, and the discoveries that mattered most came from staying — the geysers of Enceladus, caught because the orbiter flew close enough, often enough, to see a tiny moon venting its hidden ocean into space. It dropped Europe’s Huygens probe onto Titan, the only landing ever made in the outer solar system, and charted a world of methane rivers and lakes. At the end, out of fuel, it was flown deliberately into Saturn so it could never fall onto the ocean moons it had found and contaminate them — a mission that closed by protecting the places it discovered.
missions/saturn/cassini.json.description: Joint NASA-ESA-ASI mission. After a 7-year cruise using gravity assists at Venus, Earth, and Jupiter, Cassini entered Saturn orbit 2004-07-01 and operated for 13 years, completing 294 orbits and 162 close moon flybys. It discovered Enceladus’s south-polar plumes (active water-ice geysers), mapped Titan’s methane lakes via radar, and resolved Saturn’s hexagonal polar storm. The Grand Finale (April–September 2017) wove 22 orbits through the gap between the rings and the cloud tops, ending with a controlled atmospheric entry to prevent any chance of contaminating Enceladus or Titan with terrestrial microbes.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Titan IVB / Centaur lifts the combined Cassini-Huygens stack.

events.label: VENUS GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: First of four assists building the energy for Saturn arrival.

events.label: SATURN ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: Main engine burn places Cassini into Saturn orbit, beginning the 13-year tour.

missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.name: Pioneer 11
missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.first: First spacecraft to fly past Saturn (1979-09-01); demonstrated the gravity-assist that sent Voyager 2 onward
missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.dispatch: Pioneer 11 was the second scout, and it went further than its twin. After its own pass by Jupiter it used the planet’s gravity to cross the solar system and reach Saturn in 1979 — the first spacecraft ever to do so — deliberately flying through the ring plane to test whether the region was safe. It found the gap the Voyagers would thread a year later. Much of what made the Grand Tour possible was this: a small, cheap probe sent ahead to take the risks and map the hazards, so the flagships behind it could fly with confidence instead of fear.
missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.description: Twin of Pioneer 10, launched a year later. Pioneer 11 used Jupiter’s gravity to bend its trajectory toward Saturn — the canonical proof of gravity-assist propulsion, the technique that later enabled the Voyager Grand Tour. At Saturn it discovered the F ring and a small inner moon later resolved into the co-orbital pair Janus/Epimetheus. Carries the same Pioneer plaque as its twin. Signal lost 1995-09-30 from a heliocentric distance of ~43 AU; the spacecraft is now heading toward the constellation Aquila.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas-Centaur from Cape Canaveral on a Jupiter-Saturn gravity-assist trajectory.

events.label: JUPITER FLYBY
events.note: Used Jupiter assist to bend onto a Saturn-bound path.

events.label: SATURN CLOSEST APPROACH
events.note: First images of the planet at close range; discovered the F ring and a small inner moon (later resolved into the co-orbital pair Janus/Epimetheus).

missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.name: Voyager 1
missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.first: Most distant human-made object — currently ~170 AU from the Sun in interstellar space
missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.dispatch: Voyager 1 is the farthest thing humanity has ever made, and it got there almost by an accident of geometry. A close pass by Saturn’s giant moon Titan — chosen for the science — bent its path up and out of the plane of the planets and aimed it at the edge of the solar system, and it has been climbing ever since. Along the way it found active volcanoes on Io, the first ever seen off Earth, and in 1990 it turned back to take the Pale Blue Dot. In 2012 it became the first machine to cross into interstellar space. It is still transmitting, on fading nuclear power, from more than a hundred times the Earth’s distance from the Sun.
missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.description: Launched 16 days after Voyager 2, Voyager 1 flew faster and arrived at Jupiter first (1979) and Saturn first (1980). Its Titan flyby bent the trajectory upward out of the ecliptic plane, ending the planetary tour but sending it on the most direct path to the heliopause — which it crossed on 2012-08-25, the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. From a heliocentric distance of ~6 billion km it took the Pale Blue Dot family portrait (1990-02-14), the photograph Carl Sagan wrote about. Both Voyagers carry the Golden Record as humanity’s calling card.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Titan IIIE / Centaur lifts Voyager 1 from Cape Canaveral.

events.label: JUPITER CLOSEST APPROACH
events.note: Flyby at ~349,000 km; discovered Io volcanism, mapped Europa’s surface.

events.label: SATURN + TITAN FLYBYS
events.note: Titan flyby bent trajectory out of the ecliptic plane — no further planetary encounter possible.

missions/sun/parker-solar-probe.json.name: Parker Solar Probe
missions/sun/parker-solar-probe.json.first: Closest spacecraft to the Sun ever flown (6.1 M km, 9.86 R☉); first spacecraft to enter the solar corona (2021-04-28); fastest human-made object (~191 km/s)
missions/sun/parker-solar-probe.json.description: Parker Solar Probe ran the highest-energy launch ever flown for a science mission — C3 of 154 km²/s², requiring a custom Star 48BV solid third stage atop a Delta IV Heavy just to escape Earth into a Sun-falling trajectory. Seven Venus gravity assists over six years progressively lowered perihelion from 0.16 AU (P1, 2018-11-05) to 0.046 AU (P22, 2024-12-24 — 9.86 solar radii, 6.1 million km from the surface). At P8 in 2021-04-28 Parker dipped below the Alfvén critical surface — the first spacecraft ever to enter the Sun's corona. At P22 it reached ~191 km/s, becoming the fastest human-made object ever. The 11.43-cm carbon-carbon heat shield sustained 1,377 °C while the spacecraft bus 1 metre behind it remained at room temperature.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Delta IV Heavy + Star 48BV — highest C3 ever for a science mission (154 km²/s²).

events.label: VGA-1
events.note: First Venus gravity assist 2018-10-03.

events.label: P1 — FIRST PERIHELION
events.note: 2018-11-05, 0.16 AU. Closest-to-Sun ever, beating Helios 2.

events.label: P8 — CORONA ENTRY
events.note: 2021-04-28. First spacecraft to dip below the Alfvén critical surface.

events.label: VGA-6
events.note: Sixth Venus assist 2023-08-21.

events.label: P22 — DESIGN MILESTONE
events.note: 2024-12-24. 9.86 R☉ (6.1 M km from the Sun). ~191 km/s. Heat shield 1,377 °C.

missions/sun/solar-orbiter.json.name: Solar Orbiter
missions/sun/solar-orbiter.json.first: First mission designed to image the Sun's polar regions in detail; complements Parker Solar Probe's in-corona measurements with high-latitude remote sensing
missions/sun/solar-orbiter.json.description: ESA-led mission with a NASA launch and one instrument contribution. Where Parker Solar Probe goes closer than anyone has ever been, Solar Orbiter goes higher — using repeated Venus gravity assists over a decade to climb out of the ecliptic toward ~33° heliographic inclination. From that vantage point its instrument suite (PHI, EUI, SPICE, STIX, METIS, SoloHI + four in-situ packages) images the Sun's polar magnetic fields, traces solar-wind acceleration in real time, and links remote and in-situ measurements simultaneously. First perihelion 2020-06-15 at 0.51 AU. Closest perihelion to date 2022-10-12 at 0.29 AU (inside Mercury's perihelion).

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 411 from Cape Canaveral SLC-41.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: P1 — FIRST PERIHELION
events.note: 2020-06-15, 0.51 AU. Initial science begins.

events.label: VGA-2
events.note: 2022-09-04. Begins inclination climb out of the ecliptic.

events.label: P4 — CLOSEST TO DATE
events.note: 2022-10-12, 0.29 AU. Inside Mercury's perihelion.

events.label: POLAR IMAGING
events.note: Heliographic latitude exceeds 17° — first close-up polar magnetic field images.

missions/sun/ulysses.json.name: Ulysses
missions/sun/ulysses.json.first: Only spacecraft ever to enter a high-inclination heliocentric orbit; only direct measurements of the solar wind at all heliographic latitudes
missions/sun/ulysses.json.description: Joint ESA / NASA mission. Launched 1990-10-06 from STS-41 Discovery + IUS + PAM-S upper stages, Ulysses used a Jupiter gravity assist on 1992-02-08 to deflect itself ~80° out of the ecliptic — the only way to reach a near-polar Sun-relative orbit from Earth's near-equatorial orbital plane. Three full polar orbits of the Sun over 18.5 years mapped the solar wind, heliospheric magnetic field, and energetic particles at all heliographic latitudes — direct measurements that revealed how solar-wind structure varies between equatorial slow-wind regions and high-latitude fast-wind streams from coronal holes. Mission terminated 2009-06-30 when thruster hydrazine froze in the lines. Hardware remains in heliocentric polar orbit.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: STS-41 Discovery deploys Ulysses + IUS / PAM-S upper stages.

events.label: JUPITER FLYBY
events.note: Gravity assist deflects Ulysses ~80° out of the ecliptic into a polar Sun-relative orbit.

events.label: FIRST SOUTH POLAR PASS
events.note: First-ever direct measurements of solar wind over a Sun pole.

events.label: FIRST NORTH POLAR PASS
events.note: Completion of the first full solar polar orbit.

events.label: MISSION END
events.note: Thruster lines freeze; final command issued 2009-06-30.

missions/venus/akatsuki.json.name: Akatsuki
missions/venus/akatsuki.json.first: Recovered from a 5-year solar-orbit hold to achieve Venus orbit on a backup attempt; the only Venus orbiter active in its final years of operation
missions/venus/akatsuki.json.description: Akatsuki — "dawn" — was Japan's first Venus mission. Launched 2010-05-20 from Tanegashima on an H-IIA 202, paired with the IKAROS solar-sail demonstrator. The planned Venus orbit insertion 2010-12-07 failed when salt crystal buildup in an oxidiser check valve threw the main engine off-axis 152 seconds into the burn. JAXA kept the spacecraft alive in solar orbit for five years, twelve correction maneuvers, until the next Venus encounter window. On 2015-12-07 a 1228-second burn using four attitude-control thrusters — never designed for orbital insertion — placed Akatsuki into a highly elliptical 400 × 440,000 km, 3°-inclination orbit. One of the most dramatic mission-saves in spaceflight history. Contact was lost in 2024; JAXA declared operations complete on 2025-09-18.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: H-IIA 202 from Tanegashima, paired with IKAROS solar sail.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: VOI-1 FAILURE
events.note: 2010-12-07. OME throttle anomaly 152s into the burn; spacecraft sails past into solar orbit.

events.label: SOLAR-ORBIT HOLD
events.note: 12 maneuvers over 5 years to maintain a Venus re-encounter trajectory.

events.label: VOI-R2 SUCCESS
events.note: 2015-12-07. RCS-thruster 1228s burn into 400 × 440,000 km, 3° orbit.

events.label: SCIENCE OPERATIONS
events.note: UV/IR cloud-feature tracking; super-rotation studies; bow-shaped gravity waves above Aphrodite Terra. Contact lost 2024; operations declared complete 2025-09-18.

missions/venus/magellan.json.name: Magellan
missions/venus/magellan.json.first: Most complete radar map of Venus — 98% of the surface at ~120-m resolution; first planetary spacecraft launched from the Space Shuttle
missions/venus/magellan.json.description: Magellan turned Venus from a featureless cloud-veiled disc into a mapped planet. Launched from Shuttle Atlantis's payload bay 1989-05-04 — the first planetary spacecraft to ride a Shuttle — and arrived at Venus 1990-08-10 via a long Type-IV trajectory (1.5 solar revolutions). Over four mapping cycles the synthetic-aperture radar imaged 98% of Venus's surface at ~120-m resolution, revealing tessera highlands, coronae, pancake domes, and a young, volcanically-resurfaced surface. Mission ended 1994-10-13 in the Termination Experiment — the first planned controlled atmospheric entry of a planetary spacecraft.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: STS-30 / Atlantis from Kennedy LC-39B; IUS deployed from Shuttle bay.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: TCM-4
events.note: Final pre-VOI trim.

events.label: VOI
events.note: Solid-motor burn into a 295 × 8543 km, 85.5° near-polar orbit.

events.label: MAPPING CYCLE 1 COMPLETE
events.note: First full pass — 84% surface coverage at 100 m resolution.

events.label: TERMINATION EXPERIMENT
events.note: 1994-10-13. Periapsis lowered into atmosphere — first planned planetary spacecraft entry.

missions/venus/vega-1.json.name: Vega 1
missions/venus/vega-1.json.first: First-ever balloon aerostat deployed in another planet's atmosphere (Venus, 1985); first spacecraft to carry science to two distinct solar-system targets
missions/venus/vega-1.json.description: Soviet–ESA flagship of the Halley armada. Vega 1 launched 1984-12-15 with a Venera-lineage lander plus a first-of-kind ESA/CNES-built helium balloon that drifted in Venus's cloud deck at 54 km altitude for 46.5 hours, transmitting wind + temperature data via a 20-station global radio net. After dropping its descent module the bus used Venus gravity assist to redirect to comet 1P/Halley, achieving a 8890 km closest approach on 1986-03-06 — the first cometary nucleus encounter, and the position fix that ESA's Giotto used to navigate its own much closer Halley flyby a week later.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K / D-1 lifts Vega 1 from Baikonur.

events.label: VENUS ENCOUNTER
events.note: Descent module separates + lands; balloon deploys at 54 km altitude for 46.5 hours.

events.label: HALLEY FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach to comet 1P/Halley at 8890 km — first cometary nucleus observation.

missions/venus/vega-2.json.name: Vega 2
missions/venus/vega-2.json.first: First chemical analysis of Venusian highland-type soil (Aphrodite Terra, 1985); paired Halley encounter with Vega 1 fed Giotto's targeting solution
missions/venus/vega-2.json.description: Twin of Vega 1, launched 6 days later (1984-12-21) for redundancy + a paired Halley armada solution. Vega 2's descent module landed 1985-06-15 in Rusalka Planitia, on the northern flank of Aphrodite Terra, and used XRF spectrometry to find anorthosite-norite-troctolite material — the first chemical analysis of highland-type Venusian crust (the composition resembles lunar highlands, though the landing site itself is a plain). Its balloon performed identically to Vega 1's, drifting in the opposite hemisphere at ~240 km/h. The bus flew past comet 1P/Halley at 8030 km on 1986-03-09. Together the two Vega buses returned the first close-up cometary-nucleus images and refined the position fix that allowed Giotto to attempt a 596 km flyby five days later.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K / D-1 lifts Vega 2 from Baikonur 6 days behind Vega 1.

events.label: VENUS ENCOUNTER
events.note: Descent module lands at Aphrodite Terra (Rusalka Planitia) + returns first chemical analysis of highland-type Venusian crust.

events.label: HALLEY FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach to comet 1P/Halley at 8030 km — paired position fix for Giotto.

missions/venus/venera-13.json.name: Venera 13
missions/venus/venera-13.json.first: Longest surface survival of any Venus mission (127 min); first colour panoramic images and first audio from another planet's surface
missions/venus/venera-13.json.description: The peak of the Soviet Venera program. Venera 13 launched 1981-10-30 and landed 1982-03-01 at 7.5°S 303°E in the Phoebe Regio highlands. Surface conditions at touchdown: 457 °C, 89 bar, sulfuric-acid haze. The lander survived 127 minutes — nearly an hour beyond its design target — returning the first colour panoramas from another planet's surface, recording wind microphone audio, and using its drill + onboard X-ray fluorescence spectrometer to determine that the basalt at the landing site was a weakly differentiated leucite alkaline composition. Twin spacecraft Venera 14 performed identical operations at a separate site five days later. The Venera series (1967–1983) remains the only successful surface program at Venus to date.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K / D-1 lifts Venera 13 from Baikonur on a 122-day cruise.

events.label: VENUS SURFACE LANDING
events.note: Touchdown in Phoebe Regio at 7.5°S 303°E; 127 minutes of surface operations under 457 °C / 89 bar.

moon-sites/apollo11.json.name: Apollo 11
moon-sites/apollo11.json.left: Descent stage · EASEP · laser retroreflector · flag · plaque: 'We came in peace for all mankind'
moon-sites/apollo11.json.fact: The first humans on the Moon. Watched live by ~600 million people — roughly one in six people on Earth at the time. The laser retroreflector placed by Armstrong and Aldrin still receives pulses today, measuring the Earth-Moon distance to millimetre precision. Footprints in the airless regolith will survive unchanged for a million years.
moon-sites/apollo11.json.capability: First human landing — proved crewed planetary surface operations are possible. The capability ladder for Mars begins here.

moon-sites/apollo12.json.name: Apollo 12
moon-sites/apollo12.json.left: Descent stage · ALSEP · flag · retrieved parts of Surveyor 3
moon-sites/apollo12.json.fact: The precision landing — Conrad touched down within ~163 m of the uncrewed Surveyor 3 probe (1967). They retrieved pieces of it for return to Earth, showing spacecraft survive years on the Moon undamaged by radiation or micrometeorites. A proof-of-concept for future rendezvous missions.
moon-sites/apollo12.json.capability: First precision landing at a designated point — the prerequisite for any sample-return rendezvous architecture, including Mars.

moon-sites/apollo14.json.name: Apollo 14
moon-sites/apollo14.json.left: Descent stage · ALSEP · flag · two golf balls
moon-sites/apollo14.json.fact: Alan Shepard, the first American in space (1961), became the only person to play golf on the Moon. He smuggled a club head and two balls aboard. He claimed one 'went miles and miles' — LRO images suggest about 37 m (40 yards). Still: the furthest sporting achievement in history.
moon-sites/apollo14.json.capability: Demonstrated highland landing — opened scientifically valuable terrain types previously considered too hazardous, a blueprint for non-mare Mars sites.

moon-sites/apollo15.json.name: Apollo 15
moon-sites/apollo15.json.left: Descent stage · ALSEP · LRV rover · flag · Fallen Astronaut sculpture
moon-sites/apollo15.json.fact: First mission with the Lunar Roving Vehicle — drove 27.9 km. Scott left a small aluminium figurine, 'Fallen Astronaut', and a plaque listing all astronauts and cosmonauts who died in the space race. It is the only artwork on the Moon, left without public announcement at the time.
moon-sites/apollo15.json.capability: First crewed surface mobility — extended exploration radius from hundreds of metres to tens of kilometres, the model for crewed Mars surface operations.

moon-sites/apollo16.json.name: Apollo 16
moon-sites/apollo16.json.left: Descent stage · ALSEP · LRV rover · flag · Duke family photo
moon-sites/apollo16.json.fact: The only mission to land in the lunar highlands. Charles Duke left a photo of his family sealed in a bag on the lunar surface. On the back he wrote: 'This is the family of Astronaut Duke from Planet Earth. Landed on the Moon, April 1972.' It will outlast civilisation.
moon-sites/apollo16.json.capability: Highland geological sampling — diversified the lunar sample inventory beyond mare basalts and reshaped models of planetary crust formation, methods reused for Mars.

moon-sites/apollo17.json.name: Apollo 17
moon-sites/apollo17.json.left: Descent stage · ALSEP · LRV rover · flag · plaque: 'Here Man completed his first explorations of the Moon. May the spirit of peace in which we came be reflected in the lives of all mankind.'
moon-sites/apollo17.json.fact: The last time humans visited the Moon. Gene Cernan was the last person to walk on its surface. Before climbing the ladder, he said: 'We leave as we came, and God willing, we shall return.' Harrison Schmitt, the only trained geologist on the Moon, collected samples that reshaped our understanding of lunar geology.
moon-sites/apollo17.json.capability: First trained geologist on a planetary surface — set the precedent that crewed Mars missions should include scientists, not just pilots.

moon-sites/artemis3.json.name: Artemis III
crew: TBD — first woman and first person of colour on Moon
moon-sites/artemis3.json.fact: The first crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 in 1972 — a 55-year gap. Targets the south pole for its water ice deposits, which may enable refuelling for future deep space missions. Will land the first woman and first person of colour on the Moon. If it happens on schedule, it begins the sustained human presence that leads to Mars.
moon-sites/artemis3.json.capability: Human polar surface operations and in-situ resource utilisation rehearsal — the direct precursor to crewed Mars missions, which will depend on polar water ice for both consumables and propellant.

moon-sites/beresheet.json.name: Beresheet
moon-sites/beresheet.json.fact: First privately-funded lunar landing attempt — Israeli non-profit SpaceIL, 585 kg lander. Reached lunar orbit but a gyroscope failure during descent led to engine shutdown and a crash at ~150 m/s. Carrying a 'lunar library' of human knowledge etched on nickel discs, plus a sample of tardigrades — extremophiles capable of cryptobiosis — that may or may not have survived the impact. Inspired Beresheet 2 (planned).
moon-sites/beresheet.json.capability: Demonstrated that a small private team can reach the Moon. The crash itself surfaced lessons about descent-engine restart and IMU redundancy adopted by later commercial landers.

moon-sites/chandrayaan1.json.name: Chandrayaan-1
moon-sites/chandrayaan1.json.fact: India's first lunar mission. Carried NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M³) — which in 2009 returned the first orbital spectroscopic confirmation of water (H₂O and OH) widely distributed across the lunar surface, not just at the poles. Mission ended after 312 days when communications were lost; M³ data is still being analysed today.
moon-sites/chandrayaan1.json.capability: First direct global confirmation of lunar surface water; transformed every subsequent lunar resource-utilisation roadmap.

moon-sites/chandrayaan3.json.name: Chandrayaan-3
moon-sites/chandrayaan3.json.fact: First spacecraft to land near the lunar south pole — the most contested territory in current space exploration, where permanently shadowed craters harbour water ice. Pragyan made the first in-situ detection of sulfur near the lunar south pole using its LIBS instrument. India became the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon, and the first to reach the poles.
moon-sites/chandrayaan3.json.capability: Polar landing technique — Mars's south pole region (where seasonal water ice exists) becomes a destination only after the polar landing problem is solved on the Moon.

moon-sites/change1.json.name: Chang'e 1
moon-sites/change1.json.fact: China's first lunar mission. Built and operated as a deliberate precursor test for the Chang'e 3 lander — the orbital phase served as a flight-qualification rehearsal for the deep-space communications and orbital mechanics that the lander mission would depend on. Crashed into the Moon at end of life as a controlled impact-test.
moon-sites/change1.json.capability: First Chinese lunar mission; opened the Chang'e programme that delivered the only foreign sample-return missions (Chang'e 5, 6) of the 21st century.

moon-sites/change2.json.name: Chang'e 2
moon-sites/change2.json.fact: Began as a higher-resolution remap of the Moon following Chang'e 1, then repurposed for an extended deep-space mission. After completing lunar mapping in 2011, Chang'e 2 departed for Sun-Earth L2 — China's first deep-space mission — and then on to a 2012 flyby of asteroid 4179 Toutatis. Still tracked in heliocentric orbit.
moon-sites/change2.json.capability: First Chinese deep-space mission; first non-NASA-non-ESA mission to L2; first Chinese asteroid flyby.

moon-sites/change3.json.name: Chang'e 3 / Yutu
moon-sites/change3.json.fact: China's first lunar landing — the first soft landing anywhere on the Moon in 37 years. The Chang'e 3 lander is still alive, making it the longest-surviving lunar lander ever. Yutu drove 114 m before its drive mechanism failed, but its instruments continued returning science data.
moon-sites/change3.json.capability: Re-established robotic landing capability after a decades-long pause — the foundation for the sample-return missions (Chang'e 5, 6) that informed Mars Sample Return architecture.

moon-sites/change4.json.name: Chang'e 4 / Yutu-2
moon-sites/change4.json.left: Chang'e 4 lander · Yutu-2 rover (stationary since March 2024)
moon-sites/change4.json.fact: The first spacecraft to land on the Moon's far side — technically and operationally the hardest lunar landing ever attempted. Required a relay satellite (Queqiao) at L2 since the far side has no direct radio contact with Earth. Yutu-2 rover drove over 1.6 km before becoming stationary in March 2024; telemetry continued through at least September 2024. The far side had never been visited.
moon-sites/change4.json.capability: Demonstrated relay-satellite communications architecture for operations beyond direct line-of-sight — the exact pattern any Mars far-side or polar mission will need.

moon-sites/change5.json.name: Chang'e 5
moon-sites/change5.json.fact: First lunar sample return in 44 years — ending a gap since Luna 24 (1976). Returned 1.731 kg from a geologically young region (2 billion years old vs 3–4 billion for Apollo samples). Rewrote our model of lunar volcanism: the Moon was geologically active much more recently than thought.
moon-sites/change5.json.capability: Modern robotic sample return architecture — direct precursor to Mars Sample Return's lander/ascent vehicle/orbiter chain.

moon-sites/change6.json.name: Chang'e 6
moon-sites/change6.json.fact: First sample return from the lunar far side — possibly the most scientifically significant lunar mission since Apollo. Far-side material (thicker crust, older surface, different composition) was completely unstudied. These samples may finally explain why the Moon's two hemispheres are so fundamentally different.
moon-sites/change6.json.capability: Sample return from a relay-only site — combines the architectures of Chang'e 4 (far-side comms) and Chang'e 5 (sample return). The full set of capabilities for Mars Sample Return at any latitude.

moon-sites/clementine.json.name: Clementine
moon-sites/clementine.json.fact: Joint NASA/DoD Strategic Defense Initiative mission. Spent ten weeks mapping the Moon at 11 spectral bands — the first systematic global multispectral map. Bistatic radar measurements at the south pole produced the first hints of polar water ice, later confirmed by Lunar Prospector and Chandrayaan-1.
moon-sites/clementine.json.capability: First hint of lunar polar water ice — the discovery that motivated every subsequent south-pole mission, including Artemis III.

moon-sites/lro.json.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
moon-sites/lro.json.site_name: Lunar polar orbit (~50 km science phase; elliptical since 2011)
moon-sites/lro.json.fact: The longest-running active lunar orbital mission. LROC's narrow-angle camera resolves objects ≥50 cm — sharp enough to image every Apollo descent stage, both Lunokhod rover tracks, and every recent landed asset. Built the topographic and imagery base maps used by every recent Moon-landing mission. Currently mapping permanently-shadowed craters for Artemis south-pole site selection.
moon-sites/lro.json.capability: Definitive modern lunar reconnaissance — the eyes-in-the-sky for every recent Moon mission.

moon-sites/luna10.json.name: Luna 10
moon-sites/luna10.json.fact: First artificial satellite of any body other than Earth. Reached lunar orbit in April 1966 — four and a half months before NASA's Lunar Orbiter 1 — and broadcast "The Internationale" from lunar orbit during a Communist Party Congress. Ran for 56 days before its batteries died.
moon-sites/luna10.json.capability: First orbital reconnaissance of another world; opened the Soviet sequence that culminated in Luna 9 + Lunokhod.

moon-sites/luna16.json.name: Luna 16
moon-sites/luna16.json.left: Descent stage with cabling, ascent stage launch base
moon-sites/luna16.json.fact: First fully robotic sample return from another world — September 1970. Drilled into the lunar regolith with an articulated rotary drill, transferred 101 g of dust + small rock fragments into a sealed return capsule, then launched directly back to Earth without orbital rendezvous. Landed in Kazakhstan three days later. Two more Luna sample returns followed (Luna 20 in 1972, Luna 24 in 1976).
moon-sites/luna16.json.capability: Proved end-to-end robotic sample return is feasible — the capability that underwrites Mars Sample Return today.

moon-sites/luna17.json.name: Luna 17 / Lunokhod 1
moon-sites/luna17.json.fact: The first remote-controlled rover to operate on another world. Drove 10.5 km over 322 days, photographing over 20,000 images. Lost to history until 2010, when the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted it from orbit — still sitting exactly where it stopped.
moon-sites/luna17.json.capability: First teleoperated rover — established the architecture every Mars rover from Sojourner to Perseverance has built on.

moon-sites/luna21.json.name: Luna 21 / Lunokhod 2
moon-sites/luna21.json.left: Luna 21 lander + Lunokhod 2 rover (final resting position)
moon-sites/luna21.json.fact: Lunokhod 2 was the second of two Soviet lunar rovers (1973). Driven by a 5-person ground crew rotating in shifts at the IKI control centre. In 4 months it covered ~39 km — the lunar-surface distance record that stood for 41 years until NASA's Opportunity Mars rover passed it in 2014. Carried French laser retroreflectors that are still used for Earth-Moon ranging today.
moon-sites/luna21.json.capability: Long-distance teleoperated mobility — proved a remote crew can drive an unmanned vehicle across an alien surface in real time (with light-delay).

moon-sites/luna24.json.name: Luna 24
moon-sites/luna24.json.fact: The last Soviet lunar mission — and the last uncrewed Moon landing until China's Chang'e 3 in 2013: a gap of 37 years. Returned 170 g of samples including minerals containing water, foreshadowing the later discovery of lunar water ice.
moon-sites/luna24.json.capability: Demonstrated robotic sample return — the architecture Mars Sample Return is now attempting at interplanetary scale.

moon-sites/luna9.json.name: Luna 9
moon-sites/luna9.json.fact: The first spacecraft to achieve a soft landing on the Moon and transmit photographs from the surface. Nine panoramic images ended the debate about whether landers would sink into deep lunar dust. A defining moment — the Moon could be reached.
moon-sites/luna9.json.capability: First soft landing — required before any subsequent lunar surface operation, and the prerequisite proof-of-concept for every Mars lander since.

moon-sites/lunar-prospector.json.name: Lunar Prospector
moon-sites/lunar-prospector.json.fact: Direct neutron-spectrometer detection of hydrogen at both lunar poles — strong evidence for water ice in permanently-shadowed crater floors. Deliberately impacted into Shoemaker crater at end of mission, hoping the impact ejecta would confirm water; Earth-based observers detected nothing definitive (a follow-up only delivered by LCROSS in 2009).
moon-sites/lunar-prospector.json.capability: Confirmed Clementine's polar-ice hypothesis; established neutron-spectroscopy as the primary tool for lunar volatiles.

moon-sites/slim.json.name: SLIM
moon-sites/slim.json.fact: Japan's Smart Lander demonstrated pinpoint precision landing — targeting within 100 m accuracy vs the km-scale standard of all previous missions. Landed nose-down at roughly 90° from the intended attitude, leaving its solar panels initially pointing away from the Sun; operations resumed nine days later once the Sun angle shifted. Japan became the fifth nation to achieve a lunar soft landing.
moon-sites/slim.json.capability: Pinpoint landing accuracy — bridges the gap between 'we can land somewhere on this body' and 'we can land at the specific scientifically valuable rock', the precondition for surface-asset rendezvous on Mars.

moon-sites/smart-1.json.name: SMART-1
moon-sites/smart-1.json.fact: ESA's first lunar mission. Used solar-electric (ion) propulsion to spiral out from a geostationary transfer orbit to lunar capture — a 14-month, fuel-efficient transit that pioneered low-thrust trajectories for ESA's later interplanetary missions. Deliberately impacted the lunar surface in 2006 for an observed end-of-life experiment.
moon-sites/smart-1.json.capability: First operational use of ion propulsion for a lunar mission — a template for ESA's later BepiColombo and Hera deep-space missions.

orbit-regimes/GEO.json.name: Geostationary Orbit
orbit-regimes/GEO.json.story: Exactly 35,786 km up — the altitude where an orbit takes exactly 24 hours, so the satellite hangs motionless over a fixed longitude on the equator. Weather satellites stare at the same continent forever; communications satellites paint a dish-sized footprint and never move. There are no parking spaces, only parking slots — each operator gets a longitude band assigned by the ITU.
orbit-regimes/GEO.json.comparison: About 1/11th of the way to the Moon. A round-trip TV signal via GEO comsat takes ~240 ms — long enough to hear on a phone call ("satellite delay").

orbit-regimes/HEO.json.name: Highly Elliptical Orbit
orbit-regimes/HEO.json.story: Not an altitude, a shape. A long ellipse with a low perigee (close to Earth) and a very high apogee (sometimes higher than GEO). The orbiter spends most of its time near apogee, hanging slowly over high latitudes — the trick Soviet engineers used to get continuous comms over Russia's polar regions where a GEO satellite over the equator is too low on the horizon to see. Used today for missile-warning, deep-space tracking, and high-latitude broadband.
orbit-regimes/HEO.json.comparison: Apogee can reach 1/8th of the way to the Moon; perigee can graze the top of LEO. The orbiter sprints near Earth and crawls at the top.

orbit-regimes/L2.json.name: Sun–Earth L2
orbit-regimes/L2.json.story: The second Lagrange point — 1.5 million km from Earth, on the line from the Sun through Earth and out the back. The gravity of the Sun + Earth combine to keep a spacecraft station-keeping with minimal fuel. Always-night sky, always-warm Earth-facing side, the same Sun angle forever — the perfect parking spot for infrared telescopes that need to stay cold and pointed away from the Sun. JWST is parked here, in a halo orbit ~800,000 km wide.
orbit-regimes/L2.json.comparison: Four times farther than the Moon. The Sun, Earth, and Moon all sit on one side of the spacecraft, simplifying the sunshield geometry.

firsts.label: Herschel + Planck — first ESA L2 missions

orbit-regimes/LEO.json.name: Low Earth Orbit
orbit-regimes/LEO.json.story: The closest band of space — 160 to 2,000 km up. Short comms latency (~7 ms one-way), atmospheric drag still tugs at the lower edge, and the radiation belts haven't kicked in yet. Crewed spaceflight lives here for the same reasons: rescuable, reachable, and the human body tolerates a few-hundred-kilometre commute. Every space station that has ever flown has parked in LEO.
orbit-regimes/LEO.json.comparison: About 1/600th of the way to the Moon. The ISS at 408 km orbits at the same altitude as the distance from London to Geneva — laid sideways.

firsts.label: Vostok 1 — Yuri Gagarin, first crewed orbital flight (USSR)

orbit-regimes/MEO.json.name: Medium Earth Orbit
orbit-regimes/MEO.json.story: The navigation band — roughly 20,000 km up, where a constellation of 24+ satellites can paint every point on Earth with at least four simultaneously-visible spacecraft (the minimum for a 3D fix). All four major global positioning systems live here, intentionally spread across four independent regimes by their operating agencies. Above the inner Van Allen belt, below the outer one — a calm, high orbit.
orbit-regimes/MEO.json.comparison: About 1/19th of the way to the Moon. A signal from GPS takes ~67 ms to reach your phone — about 10× the LEO bounce.

firsts.label: GLONASS Block I — first Soviet GNSS satellite

orbit-regimes/MOON.json.name: Lunar Orbit
orbit-regimes/MOON.json.story: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite — 384,400 km out, tidally locked so it always shows the same face, and orbiting once every 27.3 days. Spacecraft visit on the way to lunar landings (NASA Apollo, CNSA Chang'e, ISRO Chandrayaan, JAXA SLIM) or to map the surface for future returns. The Lunar Gateway, when it flies, will be the first permanent crewed outpost beyond LEO.
orbit-regimes/MOON.json.comparison: 1,200× further than the ISS. A radio signal Earth → Moon → Earth takes ~2.6 seconds — long enough that mission controllers in Houston speak in slow, deliberate sentences.

firsts.label: Luna 1 — first to reach lunar vicinity (USSR)

orbit-regimes-explore/BELT.json.name: Asteroid Main Belt
orbit-regimes-explore/BELT.json.story: A ring of rocky leftovers between Mars and Jupiter — 2.2 to 3.2 AU. Hundreds of thousands of bodies catalogued; total estimated mass less than 4% of the Moon. Not the densely-packed asteroid field of science fiction: typical spacing between objects is about 1 million kilometres. The belt never accreted into a planet because Jupiter's gravity kept stirring the orbits, preventing collisions from sticking. Three Kirkwood gaps mark resonances with Jupiter where asteroids get cleared out.
orbit-regimes-explore/BELT.json.comparison: If you stood on Ceres (the largest body) you'd struggle to see another asteroid without a telescope. The belt's total mass is roughly the mass of Pluto.

firsts.label: Dawn — first dedicated asteroid orbiter (Vesta, USA)

orbit-regimes-explore/GIANTS.json.name: Gas + Ice Giants
orbit-regimes-explore/GIANTS.json.story: The outer planetary realm — 5 to 30 AU. Two gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) with hydrogen-helium envelopes thousands of kilometres deep above small rocky cores; two ice giants (Uranus, Neptune) with water/ammonia/methane mantles under thinner gas. Together they hold 99% of all planetary mass in the solar system. Each has its own moon system that reads as a miniature solar system in itself — Jupiter alone has 95 known moons, including four bigger than Pluto.
orbit-regimes-explore/GIANTS.json.comparison: Jupiter is 318× more massive than Earth. The four giants together would form a system 25× the diameter of the inner planets combined.

residents.label: Neptune — 30.07 AU, fastest winds in system

orbit-regimes-explore/HELIOPAUSE.json.name: Heliopause + Interstellar Space
orbit-regimes-explore/HELIOPAUSE.json.story: The boundary where the Sun's solar wind loses its battle against the interstellar medium — roughly 120 AU out. Inside lies the heliosphere, a bubble of charged solar particles streaming outward at hundreds of km/s. Beyond it: the cold, dense gas and cosmic rays of the galaxy itself. The Voyager probes are the only artefacts humanity has ever placed across this boundary — Voyager 1 crossed in 2012, Voyager 2 in 2018. Both still transmit data, faintly, from interstellar space.
orbit-regimes-explore/HELIOPAUSE.json.comparison: About 4× farther than Neptune. A signal from Voyager 1 takes ~22 hours to reach Earth. The probes will not encounter another star for 40,000+ years (Voyager 1 will pass within 1.6 light-years of Gliese 445 in ~40,000 years).

firsts.label: Voyager 1 crosses the heliopause — first artefact in interstellar space (USA)

orbit-regimes-explore/KUIPER.json.name: Kuiper Belt
orbit-regimes-explore/KUIPER.json.story: A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune — 30 to 50 AU. The frozen analog of the asteroid belt: hundreds of thousands of bodies of which only the largest few have been resolved. Composed of methane, ammonia, water ice + rock. Pluto was the first member identified, in 1930, though the belt wasn't recognised as a population until the 1990s when Jewitt + Luu found the second member (1992 QB1). New Horizons gave humanity its first close looks at TWO Kuiper objects — Pluto in 2015 and Arrokoth in 2019.
orbit-regimes-explore/KUIPER.json.comparison: If the asteroid belt is a thin ring around the inner solar system, the Kuiper belt is 1,000× wider and contains ~25× more mass. Sunlight at Pluto is 1/1,600th its strength at Earth.

firsts.label: Pluto discovered — first KBO identified (Tombaugh, USA)
New Horizons at Arrokoth — most distant body ever visited (USA)

orbit-regimes-explore/OORT.json.name: Oort Cloud
orbit-regimes-explore/OORT.json.story: A hypothetical spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the entire solar system — extending from roughly 2,000 to 100,000 AU. Never directly observed, only inferred: the long-period comets we see have orbits so wide they must come from out here. Estimated population: trillions of bodies. The Oort cloud represents the solar system's birth-cloud leftovers, dynamically stable for billions of years at this distance from the Sun. Passing stars can perturb individual objects inward, becoming the comets we observe.
orbit-regimes-explore/OORT.json.comparison: Half a light-year out. The Sun's gravitational reach extends roughly to the inner Oort cloud edge — beyond that, the galaxy's tides start to dominate. The Voyagers will take 30,000 years just to reach the inner boundary.

orbit-regimes-explore/SCATTERED.json.name: Scattered Disc + Sednoids
orbit-regimes-explore/SCATTERED.json.story: Bodies on highly elliptical orbits beyond the Kuiper Belt — 50 to 1,000 AU. They were likely scattered out here by gravitational interactions with Neptune long ago. Sedna is the prototype Sednoid: 76 AU at perihelion, 937 AU at aphelion, an 11,400-year orbit. Their orbits are too far for Neptune to have placed them currently, hinting at influences from passing stars, a hypothetical Planet Nine, or the Sun's lost siblings from its birth cluster. No spacecraft has ever visited.
orbit-regimes-explore/SCATTERED.json.comparison: Sedna at aphelion sits 1/53rd of the way to the Sun's nearest stellar neighbour, Proxima Centauri. The light reaching Sedna from the Sun is 1/350,000th of what hits Earth.

orbit-regimes-explore/SUN.json.name: The Sun
orbit-regimes-explore/SUN.json.story: The centre of the solar system — a G2V main-sequence star, 4.6 billion years old, fusing 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second. Holds 99.86% of the system's total mass; everything else is leftover dust. Surface temperature ~5,500°C; core ~15 million°C. The photosphere is what we see; the corona stretches millions of kilometres beyond it and reaches ~1 million°C — one of physics's open mysteries (why is the corona hotter than the surface?).
orbit-regimes-explore/SUN.json.comparison: Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes 17 seconds to reach Earth — a snapshot of how the Sun was 8 minutes ago. The Sun is 333,000× more massive than Earth.

firsts.label: Parker Solar Probe — closest-ever Sun flyby (USA)

orbit-regimes-explore/TERRESTRIAL.json.name: Inner Terrestrial Planets
orbit-regimes-explore/TERRESTRIAL.json.story: The rocky inner solar system — 0.4 to 1.5 AU from the Sun. Four small worlds with metallic cores, silicate mantles, and thin or no atmospheres. They formed inside the frost line, where it was too hot for volatile ices to condense, so only refractory materials (silicates, iron, nickel) stayed solid. Three of the four have been targets of crewed exploration (Earth, Moon, Mars-bound).
orbit-regimes-explore/TERRESTRIAL.json.comparison: All four terrestrials would fit inside Jupiter's Great Red Spot. The four together hold less than 0.5% of the system's planetary mass.

orbit-regimes-mars/AREOSTATIONARY.json.name: Areostationary Orbit
orbit-regimes-mars/AREOSTATIONARY.json.story: The Mars equivalent of geostationary — 17,031 km up, where an orbit takes exactly one Martian sidereal day (24 h 37 min 22 s), so a spacecraft would hang motionless over a fixed Martian longitude. No spacecraft has ever used this orbit. It's the design target for future Mars relay constellations: as crewed missions and surface bases grow, parking communications satellites in areostationary slots would mirror Earth's GEO comsat network, eliminating the daily comms outages that today's low-orbit relays impose on every surface mission.
orbit-regimes-mars/AREOSTATIONARY.json.comparison: Just below Mars's outer moon Deimos (23,460 km). Three areostationary satellites spaced 120° apart would cover the entire Martian disc — the same trick GEO comsats use for Earth broadcast TV.

orbit-regimes-mars/DMO.json.name: Deep Mars Orbit
orbit-regimes-mars/DMO.json.story: Above areostationary, in the 20,000-43,000 km elliptical band. The UAE's Hope orbiter is the only spacecraft here — its 55-hour orbit takes a wide elliptical path designed for global atmospheric science: hovering near apoapsis lets it watch entire weather systems develop and decay across the planet's full day-night terminator. Deimos, the outer Martian moon, also orbits within this band at 23,460 km.
orbit-regimes-mars/DMO.json.comparison: Hope's apoapsis at 43,000 km is about 1/9th the way to Phobos's distance from Earth's Moon. The orbit was deliberately chosen to be UNIQUE in the Mars fleet — no other spacecraft sees the planet from this angle.

firsts.label: Hope — first UAE mission to another planet

orbit-regimes-mars/HILL.json.name: Martian Hill Sphere
orbit-regimes-mars/HILL.json.story: The outer limit of Mars's gravitational authority — about 1.08 million kilometres from the planet's centre. Inside this sphere, Mars's gravity wins over the Sun's; outside, the Sun reclaims anything you leave behind. Mars's Hill sphere is smaller than Earth's (1.5 M km) because Mars has less mass, even though Mars sits farther from the Sun. Both Martian moons orbit deep inside (Deimos at 2% of the Hill radius). No spacecraft has been placed near the boundary.
orbit-regimes-mars/HILL.json.comparison: Roughly the distance from Earth to the Earth-Moon L2 Lagrange point. Anything captured into a Mars-bound trajectory has to dump enough energy to stay inside this boundary, or the Sun will pull it back into solar orbit.

orbit-regimes-mars/HMO.json.name: High Mars Orbit
orbit-regimes-mars/HMO.json.story: Highly elliptical orbits in the 1,000-2,500 km range, mostly historic. Mariner 9 made it here in 1971 — the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, beating Mars 2 by a few weeks. The Soviet Mars 3 and the American Viking 1 orbiters followed, all parked in long ellipses that minimised station-keeping fuel during the Mariner-era of limited delta-v budgets. Phobos passes through this band at 9,376 km — Viking and Mars Express both used the geometry to study the moon up close.
orbit-regimes-mars/HMO.json.comparison: Roughly the altitude where Earth's GPS satellites orbit — but around a planet just over half Earth's size. The orbiter's view of Mars at apoapsis is the classic 'whole-disc' framing in early 1970s mission photographs.

firsts.label: Mariner 9 — first artificial satellite of any planet other than Earth (USA)

orbit-regimes-mars/LMO.json.name: Low Mars Orbit
orbit-regimes-mars/LMO.json.story: The mapping band — typically 150 to 500 km above the Martian surface. Most Mars orbiters live here: it's high enough to dodge the atmospheric drag from the upper thermosphere yet low enough for metre-scale imaging. The thin atmosphere is a gift — Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Mars Odyssey have used aerobraking (dipping repeatedly through it) to circularise their orbits for free, saving years of propellant. Six nations are flying spacecraft here right now.
orbit-regimes-mars/LMO.json.comparison: About 1/9th the distance from Mars to Phobos. From LMO you can resolve a tennis court on the surface (HiRISE on MRO does 25 cm/px).

residents.label: Mars Express — first ESA Mars mission

firsts.label: Mars Express — first ESA Mars mission

orbit-regimes-moon/HILL.json.name: Lunar Hill Sphere
orbit-regimes-moon/HILL.json.story: The boundary of the Moon's gravitational authority — roughly 60,000 km from the lunar centre. Inside this sphere, the Moon's gravity wins out over Earth's; outside, anything you leave behind drifts back toward Earth. Most stable lunar orbits live well inside, below 70% of the Hill radius, because mascon perturbation makes higher orbits unstable. The Hill sphere is also why the Moon has no natural moonlets — none can hold an orbit for long.
orbit-regimes-moon/HILL.json.comparison: About 16% of the way back to Earth. The Earth-Moon L2 point sits roughly on the Hill sphere boundary on the far side — the same geometric reason both exist.

orbit-regimes-moon/HLO.json.name: High Lunar Orbit
orbit-regimes-moon/HLO.json.story: Elliptical mapping orbits and parking trajectories above 100 km. The 1966 Luna 10 was placed here — the first artefact to enter orbit around any body other than Earth. SMART-1 lingered in highly elliptical orbits to test ion propulsion endurance. Most modern lunar missions transit through HLO before lowering into LLO; some end their life by being raised here to free up the LLO 'workspace' before disposal impact.
orbit-regimes-moon/HLO.json.comparison: Roughly the altitude of GEO above Earth, but around a body 27% the diameter. The lunar horizon recedes; the spacecraft sees a full lunar disc instead of close-up surface.

orbit-regimes-moon/L2.json.name: Earth-Moon L2
orbit-regimes-moon/L2.json.story: The Lagrange point 64,500 km behind the Moon as seen from Earth — the gravitational saddle where Earth, Moon, and centrifugal forces balance. The Moon always sits between the spacecraft and Earth, so direct comms are impossible — but a satellite parked here in a halo orbit AROUND L2 has line-of-sight to BOTH the lunar farside AND Earth. That's how China landed Chang'e 4 on the farside in 2019: the Queqiao relay satellite, parked in a halo around Earth-Moon L2, bridges every command and image.
orbit-regimes-moon/L2.json.comparison: About 1/6th the distance from Earth to the Moon. Without a relay at L2, the entire lunar farside is a comms blackout — every spacecraft that ever landed there has needed one.

firsts.label: Queqiao — first operational Earth-Moon L2 relay (China)

orbit-regimes-moon/LLO.json.name: Low Lunar Orbit
orbit-regimes-moon/LLO.json.story: The closest band to the lunar surface — typically 50 to 100 km up. Spacecraft here can image the surface at sub-metre resolution but pay a steep price: the Moon's mass distribution is wildly uneven (giant subsurface mascons under the maria), so a low orbit perturbs aggressively. Most LLO missions need active station-keeping or a carefully chosen 'frozen' inclination that resists the drift. LRO has flown here continuously since 2009 — the longest-lived lunar mission.
orbit-regimes-moon/LLO.json.comparison: About 1/3,800th of the way back to Earth. From LLO the Moon's horizon is sharply curved — you can see 30-40 km in any direction before the surface drops off.

orbit-regimes-moon/NRHO.json.name: Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit
orbit-regimes-moon/NRHO.json.story: Not really an orbit around the Moon — more like a long figure-8 around the Earth-Moon L1 and L2 Lagrange points, dipping close to the lunar south pole at perilune (~3,000 km) and stretching far above the north pole at apolune (~70,000 km). The geometry has two prizes: continuous line-of-sight back to Earth (no comms blackout) and very low station-keeping fuel — a few m/s per year. NASA's Lunar Gateway, when it flies, will live in NRHO. CAPSTONE flew there in 2022 as a pathfinder.
orbit-regimes-moon/NRHO.json.comparison: An NRHO completes one loop every ~7 days — roughly a quarter of the Moon's own orbital period. The spacecraft is always close to the south-pole region but never directly above it.

planets/arrokoth.json.name: Arrokoth
planets/arrokoth.json.type: Kuiper Belt Object · Cold-classical · Contact binary
planets/arrokoth.json.fact: The most distant body ever visited by a spacecraft — 4.1 billion km from the Sun when New Horizons flew within 3,500 km on New Year's Day 2019. Its two lobes (Wenu and Weeyo) gently merged at the dawn of the solar system and have stayed merged for 4.5 billion years at ~40 K.
planets/arrokoth.json.bio: Discovered in 2014 by Hubble and originally catalogued as 2014 MU69. Renamed Arrokoth (Powhatan for 'sky') in 2019 after the New Horizons flyby — a pristine remnant of the planetesimal disk preserved unmodified since formation. Its red, gently-accreted contact-binary shape is a direct fingerprint of how planet-building started in the outer solar system.

links.l: Arrokoth's gentle origins (NASA / Stern et al., Science 2020)

planets/didymos.json.name: Didymos
planets/didymos.json.fact: Parent of the 160-m moonlet Dimorphos struck by NASA's DART on 2022-09-26 — the first demonstration of kinetic-impactor planetary defense. Didymos itself remained intact as a 780-m S-type observing the binary period change.
planets/didymos.json.bio: S-type near-Earth binary discovered 1996, with the 160-m moonlet Dimorphos in an 11.9-hour orbit at 1.2-km separation. Classified as a chondritic body — LL-class silicate composition, common in the inner main belt. ESA's Hera mission (launched 2024) will arrive 2026 to survey the post-impact system in detail.

planets/dimorphos.json.name: Dimorphos
planets/dimorphos.json.fact: The first celestial body whose orbit was deliberately altered by humans. NASA's DART struck Dimorphos at 6.14 km/s on 2022-09-26, shortening its 11.9-hour orbit around Didymos by 33 minutes (4.2%) — exceeding the success threshold by ~25× and demonstrating planetary defense is possible.
planets/dimorphos.json.bio: 160-m moonlet of 65803 Didymos, discovered 2003. The DART surface turned out to be 'rubble-pile fluid' — the spacecraft sank ~50 cm into the surface during the half-second of contact, and the momentum-transfer enhancement factor β ≈ 3.6 indicated significant carry from ejected surface material. The CubeSat LICIACube imaged the plume in real time; HST and JWST observed the ejecta tail for weeks.

links.l: Daly et al. (2023) — Successful kinetic impact (Nature)

planets/donaldjohanson.json.name: Donaldjohanson
planets/donaldjohanson.json.fact: A 4-km main-belt C-type named for the discoverer of the Lucy hominid fossil. Added late in Lucy's mission design as a bonus en-route flyby (2025-04-20, 920 km closest approach at 13.4 km/s) — a chance to test instruments before the harder Trojan encounters.
planets/donaldjohanson.json.bio: Discovered 1981, located in the inner main belt. The dual etymology — Donald Johanson (paleoanthropologist) → Lucy fossil → Lucy spacecraft — makes the asteroid a deliberate naming gesture toward the mission's evolutionary-deep-history theme: Trojans preserve early-solar-system material the way the fossil preserves early-human history.

planets/earth.json.name: Earth
planets/earth.json.fact: Every human who has ever lived did so here. The reference orbit by which all others are measured.
planets/earth.json.bio: The 23.44° axial tilt creates the seasons — not distance from the Sun. Earth is actually closer to the Sun in January than July.

links.l: Why Earth has seasons (NASA Climate Kids)
Pale Blue Dot — Carl Sagan reflection (Planetary Society)

science_sections.why: The astronomical unit IS the Earth-Sun mean distance — Earth is the literal yardstick for every solar-system measurement.
Earth's orbit defines the ecliptic plane. Every other planet's inclination is measured relative to this reference.
Earth's 23.4° tilt is the textbook seasons-machine — equinoxes and solstices arise directly from the angle between rotation axis and orbital plane.
Every Mars launch window — every 26 months — is an Earth-departure Hohmann transfer. The ladder leaves from here.
The Moon is unusually large for its parent — the ratio (diameter ≈ 0.27 of Earth) is the highest in any planet–satellite pair.

planets/eurybates.json.name: Eurybates
planets/eurybates.json.fact: Largest member of the L4 Eurybates Trojan family — a collisional cluster of 64-km parent and ~280 smaller fragments. Lucy's 2027-08-12 encounter at 5.7 km/s will be the first close-up of a Jupiter Trojan ever, accompanied by Eurybates's 1-km moon Queta (discovered by Hubble in 2018).
planets/eurybates.json.bio: Named for the Greek herald of Odysseus (Iliad / Odyssey), discovered 1973.
