Two five-segment solid rocket boosters and a core stage with four RS-25 engines (the same engines that flew on Space Shuttle), topped by an Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage. Debuted on Artemis I (Nov 2022), sending an uncrewed Orion capsule around the Moon.

rockets/soyuz-fregat.json.name: Soyuz-FG / Fregat
rockets/soyuz-fregat.json.first: The launcher that put every Mars Express, Cluster, and ESA-Roscosmos joint mission on its way
rockets/soyuz-fregat.json.description: Soyuz-FG (now retired) plus the Fregat upper stage — the standard ESA-Roscosmos pairing for medium interplanetary missions. The cryogenic-free design uses kerosene-LOX in the lower stages and Fregat's restartable hypergolic propellants for precise injection. Launched ESA's Mars Express (2003), the Cluster magnetospheric quartet, and most pre-Soyuz-2 ISS resupply flights.

rockets/starship.json.name: Starship
rockets/starship.json.first: First fully reusable orbital launch system, designed for Mars settlement
rockets/starship.json.description: Two-stage stainless-steel vehicle with a Super Heavy booster (33 Raptor engines) and a Starship upper stage (6 Raptors). Architected around orbital propellant transfer: a tanker variant refills Starship in LEO, enabling ~100 t to Mars surface — orders of magnitude more than any prior launcher. Orbital flight programme began 2023.

satellites/ariel.json.description: The brightest and (after Miranda) youngest-looking surface in the Uranian system — Voyager 2 imagery shows broad rift valleys and what may be flow features hinting at past or present cryovolcanic activity. Tidal heating from a 2:1 orbital resonance with Umbriel that existed in the deep past could have melted the interior; whether any liquid water remains today is unknown. Like the other Uranian major moons, only its southern hemisphere has been imaged at close range.
satellites/ariel.json.surface_composition: Water-ice crust + silicate / carbonaceous rock interior; surface the brightest of Uranus's major moons, with relatively few craters — interpreted as evidence of cryovolcanic resurfacing within the last ~1 Gyr.

science_sections.why: Ariel orbits at 190,900 km from Uranus — second-innermost of the major moons. Like all Uranian moons, its orbit shares the planet's 97° axial tilt.

satellites/callisto.json.description: Callisto sits outside the Laplace resonance that drives the tidal heating in Io, Europa, and Ganymede — so its interior never melted enough to differentiate fully or resurface its crust. The result is the most pristine record of impact bombardment in the inner Galilean system, including the spectacular Valhalla basin's 15-ring system stretching nearly half the moon's circumference. Despite the lack of tidal heating, Galileo's magnetometer detected an induced magnetic field consistent with a deep salty ocean ~100 km below the surface. Its low radiation environment (compared to Europa or Ganymede) and long-lived water make it a likely staging point for future crewed missions to the Jupiter system.
satellites/callisto.json.surface_composition: Roughly 40% water ice + 60% silicate rock; surface the most heavily-cratered in the solar system — almost saturated, untouched by resurfacing. Notable feature: the 3,800 km Valhalla multi-ring impact basin.
mission_visits: Galileo orbiter — USA, 1995–2003 (multiple flybys; ocean candidate)

science_sections.why: Callisto orbits outside the Laplace resonance — its 1.88-million-km semi-major axis puts it beyond the worst of Jupiter's radiation belts, making it the most spacecraft-friendly Galilean.
Callisto's 0.007 eccentricity is small and unforced — without resonant pumping, no tidal flexing, no subsurface ocean (probably).

satellites/charon.json.description: Half Pluto's diameter — the largest moon-to-planet size ratio in the solar system. Charon and Pluto are mutually tidally locked, orbiting a common centre of mass 1,700 km above Pluto's surface — effectively a binary planet system. New Horizons revealed a startlingly varied terrain: the smooth Vulcan Planitia plain to the south, an ancient cratered hemisphere to the north, and a dark red polar cap (Mordor Macula) of tholins formed when methane molecules escaping from Pluto's atmosphere collected on Charon and were processed by ultraviolet light. The four smaller Pluto moons (Styx, Nix, Kerberos, Hydra) orbit the Pluto-Charon barycentre with chaotic rotations driven by the binary system's shifting gravity.
satellites/charon.json.surface_composition: Water-ice crust with ammonia hydrates and tholins; the dark reddish polar cap (Mordor Macula) is methane gas escaped from Pluto and processed into tholins on Charon's frigid surface.
mission_visits: New Horizons — USA, 2015 (first and only flyby)

science_sections.why: Charon and Pluto orbit a barycentre that sits OUTSIDE Pluto — making it the only known true binary system in the solar system rather than a planet-with-moon.
Charon's 19,591-km mean distance from Pluto, combined with mutual tidal locking, means both bodies show the same face to each other forever.

satellites/deimos.json.description: The smaller and outer of Mars's two moons, just 12 km across — the smallest known body in the solar system that still resolves as a disc rather than a point from a typical orbital camera. Its smoother surface (compared to Phobos's crater-grooved terrain) and slower orbit (30 hours vs Phobos's 8) make it the more sedate of Mars's moon pair. Asaph Hall named both moons for the Greek personifications of Fear (Phobos) and Dread (Deimos) — the war horses pulling Ares's chariot in Iliad XV.
satellites/deimos.json.surface_composition: Carbonaceous chondrite-like; smoother surface than Phobos because its weaker gravity lets ejecta from impacts escape into Mars orbit rather than re-accumulating. Two named craters: Swift and Voltaire (both ~3 km).
mission_visits: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter — USA, 2009 (HiRISE close pass)

science_sections.why: Deimos is the outer Mars moon (23,460 km) — its orbital period (1.26 d) is longer than the Martian day, so tidal forces are pushing it slowly outward.

satellites/enceladus.json.description: Tiny — just 504 km across — but the most reflective body in the solar system and one of the strongest candidates for present-day habitability beyond Earth. Cassini flew directly through plumes erupting from four 130-km-long fractures at the south pole; the spectrometer detected molecular hydrogen, organics including methane, salts, and silica nanograins indicating active hydrothermal chemistry on the ocean floor. The ocean is in direct contact with rocky seafloor — the same energy and chemistry conditions that gave rise to life at Earth's own deep-sea hydrothermal vents.
satellites/enceladus.json.surface_composition: Pristine water-ice crust over a global subsurface ocean; south-polar 'tiger stripe' fractures venting plumes of water vapour, organics, salts, silica nanograins, and molecular hydrogen.

science_sections.why: Enceladus is in 2:1 mean-motion resonance with Dione — the forced eccentricity (0.0047) drives the tidal flexing that powers the south-polar cryovolcanic plumes.

satellites/europa.json.description: Smoothest large body in the solar system — no mountain on Europa rises higher than a few hundred metres. Beneath its 20-km ice crust lies a global salt-water ocean ~100 km deep, holding more than twice the water in all of Earth's oceans combined. Tidal flexing from Jupiter keeps that ocean liquid and chemically active; magnetic-field signatures and Hubble observations of plumes suggest material from the subsurface ocean reaches the surface periodically. NASA's Europa Clipper (en route) and ESA's JUICE will both scrutinise the ice shell and ocean dynamics through the early 2030s.
satellites/europa.json.surface_composition: Water-ice crust ~15–25 km thick, fractured by chaos terrain into a network of arcuate ridges and lenticulae; salts (likely magnesium sulfate + sodium chloride) tint the ice red-brown in the chaos regions.

library_labels.europa-juice: ESA JUICE — Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer

science_sections.why: Europa is the middle member of the Io–Europa–Ganymede 4:2:1 Laplace resonance — its forced eccentricity drives the tidal flexing that keeps a subsurface ocean liquid.
Europa's tiny 0.009 eccentricity is forced by Io's perturbations — without it the subsurface ocean would freeze. Europa Clipper (NASA, 2024–) is launching to study it.

satellites/ganymede.json.description: The solar system's largest moon — bigger than Mercury, 8% larger than the Moon. Ganymede is the only moon with a self-generated magnetic field, evidence of a partially-molten iron core. Beneath ~150 km of ice lies a saltwater ocean larger than all of Earth's oceans combined; some models suggest a layered structure with multiple oceans separated by ice phases of different densities. ESA's JUICE mission will become the first orbiter of a moon other than Earth's when it enters Ganymede orbit in December 2034.
satellites/ganymede.json.surface_composition: Roughly half water ice + half silicate rock; surface a mix of dark cratered terrain (~4 Gyr old) and lighter grooved terrain (tectonic resurfacing ~2 Gyr ago); thin oxygen exosphere.

science_sections.why: Ganymede is the only moon in the solar system with its own internally-generated magnetic field — produced by an iron-rich core embedded in Jupiter's magnetosphere.
Outer member of the 4:2:1 Laplace resonance with Io and Europa — Ganymede's stability anchors the whole inner-Galilean system.

satellites/io.json.description: The most geologically active body in the solar system. Tidal heating from Jupiter's gravity plus orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede pumps roughly 100 terawatts of heat into Io's interior — enough to drive ~400 simultaneously-active volcanoes and surface temperatures that swing from -130 °C (frozen sulfur dioxide) to +1,600 °C (ultra-mafic lava). Its surface is repainted faster than impact cratering can mark it. Loki Patera, a 200 km lava lake, is the single most powerful volcanic feature in the solar system.
satellites/io.json.surface_composition: Sulfur + sulfur-dioxide frost over silicate crust; surface paint regularly resurfaced by volcanic flows — no impact craters survive long enough to be visible.

library_labels.io-juno: NASA Juno — recent close flybys of Io

science_sections.why: Io / Europa / Ganymede are locked in a 4:2:1 Laplace resonance — for every 4 Io orbits, Europa makes 2 and Ganymede 1. The resonance keeps Io's orbit non-circular.
Io's tidal heating (which makes it the most volcanically active world in the solar system) comes from forced eccentricity — pumped by Europa and Ganymede through the Laplace resonance.

satellites/miranda.json.description: The innermost and smallest of Uranus's five major moons — and visually the most extreme. Voyager 2's flyby imagery revealed a surface that looks like it was assembled from mismatched pieces: enormous cliffs, fractured plateaus, and concentric coronae jutting from heavily-cratered older terrain. The leading hypothesis is that Miranda was disrupted by an impact at least once, with the fragments reassembling under their own gravity. Verona Rupes drops ~20 km — under Miranda's low gravity, a falling object would take roughly 12 minutes to reach the bottom.
satellites/miranda.json.surface_composition: Water-ice + silicate rock; surface a patchwork of ancient cratered terrain crossed by huge coronae — concentric ridges and grooves that include Verona Rupes, the tallest known cliff in the solar system (~20 km vertical drop).
mission_visits: Voyager 2 — USA, 1986 (only spacecraft visit; southern-hemisphere flyby)

science_sections.why: Miranda has the highest orbital inclination (4.3°) of the major Uranian moons — combined with an early-system disruption event, it explains the famous cliff faces Voyager 2 imaged in 1986.

satellites/moon.json.description: Earth's only natural satellite and the only world other than Earth that humans have walked on. Its 1:1 tidal lock keeps the same hemisphere facing Earth at all times — the near side dominated by lava-flooded mare basins, the far side an ancient highland-cratered terrain crowned by the South Pole–Aitken basin, the largest impact structure in the solar system (~2,500 km wide, ~13 km deep). The Moon's slow recession from Earth (~3.8 cm/year) is gradually lengthening Earth's day; in the distant past it appeared nearly three times its current angular size in the sky.
satellites/moon.json.surface_composition: Anorthosite highlands (calcium-aluminium silicates) + basaltic mare flooded by ancient lava; regolith depth 4–15 m; trace water ice in permanently-shadowed polar craters.
mission_visits: Luna 2 — USSR, 1959 (first artificial object on the Moon)

library_labels.moon-lroc: LROC — Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera image archive

science_sections.why: The Moon's orbit around Earth is the textbook two-body Keplerian system — every other moon-around-planet calculation generalises from here.
The Moon's 0.055 eccentricity is small but matters — at perigee the disc looks 12 % larger and brighter than at apogee ('supermoon').
Perigee (~363,000 km) and apogee (~405,000 km) drive the Moon's apparent size and the tidal-bulge phase that pulls the most water on Earth.
The Moon is unusually large relative to Earth — its diameter ratio (≈ 0.27) is the highest of any planet–satellite pair in the solar system.

satellites/oberon.json.description: The outermost of Uranus's major moons. Oberon's surface is heavily cratered and reddish-tinged — older than Titania's, with no clear evidence of resurfacing since the late heavy bombardment ~4 Gyr ago. Several large craters have notably dark floors; spectra are consistent with hydrocarbon residues left by space-weathered organics. A 6 km mountain — possibly the central peak of a large impact basin — rises near the limb in Voyager 2's best image.
satellites/oberon.json.surface_composition: Water-ice + silicate rock; reddish-tinged ancient cratered surface; the dark floors of several large craters are coated in unidentified dark material, possibly hydrocarbons or carbonates.

science_sections.why: Oberon is the outermost of the five major Uranian moons (583,500 km orbit) — its surface is the most cratered, suggesting it has the oldest exposed surface in the Uranus system.

satellites/phobos.json.description: The larger and inner of Mars's two moons — irregular potato-shaped body just 22 km across at its widest. Phobos orbits Mars every 7 hours 39 minutes, faster than Mars itself rotates, so from the Martian surface it rises in the west and sets in the east twice per Martian day. Its orbit is decaying at ~2 cm per year; in 30–50 million years tidal forces will either tear it apart into a temporary ring or crash it into the planet. Japan's MMX mission (launch ~2026) will return surface samples.
satellites/phobos.json.surface_composition: Heavily-cratered carbonaceous chondrite-like body, possibly a captured asteroid or accretion remnant; surface dominated by the 9 km Stickney crater and parallel grooves likely tied to ejecta from that impact.
mission_visits: Mars Express — ESA, 2010 (sub-100 m altitude flyby)

library_labels.phobos-mmx: JAXA MMX — sample-return mission to Phobos
library_labels.phobos-hirise: HiRISE — Phobos at 0.25 m/px from Mars orbit

science_sections.why: Phobos orbits Mars at just 9,377 km — below the synchronous altitude, so it is tidally accelerated INWARD and will impact Mars in ~40 million years.
Phobos's perihelion-aphelion swing is tiny but it circles Mars three times per Martian day — the most-orbits-per-parent-day moon in the system.

satellites/titan.json.description: Second-largest moon in the solar system and the only moon with a substantial atmosphere — thicker than Earth's. Below the orange tholin haze sits the only known body besides Earth with stable liquid on its surface: hydrocarbon lakes and seas of methane and ethane in the polar regions, fed by an active methane hydrologic cycle that includes clouds, rain, and rivers carving water-ice bedrock. Huygens (ESA) made the first landing on a moon other than Earth's in 2005. NASA's Dragonfly will arrive in 2034 as a nuclear-powered rotorcraft, hopping between Titan's organic-rich landscapes.
satellites/titan.json.surface_composition: Water-ice bedrock under organic dunes + hydrocarbon lakes (methane / ethane) + a nitrogen-methane atmosphere 1.45× Earth's sea-level pressure. Tholin haze tints the sky orange.

library_labels.titan-dragonfly: NASA Dragonfly — nuclear rotorcraft mission to Titan
library_labels.titan-huygens: ESA Huygens — first landing on a moon other than ours

science_sections.why: Titan is in 1:1 spin-orbit resonance with Saturn — always shows the same face. Its 1.22-million-km semi-major axis places it near Saturn's outer Hill sphere.
Titan has a dense N₂-CH₄ atmosphere — the only moon with one. Surface temperatures sit at 94 K, where methane and ethane exist as liquid lakes.

satellites/titania.json.description: The largest moon of Uranus and eighth-largest in the solar system. Voyager 2 imagery revealed a surface cut by enormous canyon systems — Messina Chasma alone stretches 1,500 km across the southern hemisphere — alongside large impact basins and the small fresh-looking Ursula crater. A 2017 stellar occultation tentatively detected a thin carbon-dioxide atmosphere, which would be the first atmosphere found on a Uranian moon.
satellites/titania.json.surface_composition: Water-ice + silicate rock; ancient cratered terrain cut by vast canyon systems hundreds of kilometres long — Messina Chasma stretches ~1,500 km across the moon.

science_sections.why: Titania is the largest moon of Uranus (1,578 km diameter) — comparable in size to Pluto. Only Voyager 2 has imaged it (1986).

satellites/triton.json.description: Neptune's largest moon and one of the most geologically active worlds in the solar system. Triton orbits Neptune backwards (retrograde) and at an extreme tilt — diagnostic of a captured Kuiper Belt object, making it likely a sibling of Pluto rather than a native Neptunian moon. Voyager 2 detected active nitrogen geysers venting dark organic dust 8 km into a tenuous nitrogen atmosphere; the southern hemisphere features 'cantaloupe terrain' — a network of dimples and ridges seen nowhere else in the solar system. Triton's retrograde orbit is decaying tidally; in roughly 3.6 Gyr it will either be torn into a Saturn-like ring or crash into Neptune.
satellites/triton.json.surface_composition: Frozen nitrogen + water ice + carbon dioxide ice; surface covered with cantaloupe-textured terrain unique in the solar system, and active nitrogen cryogeysers venting dark plumes 8 km into a thin nitrogen atmosphere.

science_sections.why: Triton's 156.8° orbital inclination — retrograde, steeply tilted to Neptune's equator — is the smoking-gun for capture from the Kuiper Belt rather than formation with Neptune.
Triton's tidal drag is decreasing its orbit — in 3.6 billion years it will either impact Neptune or fragment inside the Roche limit and form a ring system.

satellites/umbriel.json.description: Umbriel is the dark twin in the Uranian system — about the same size as Ariel but reflecting less than half the sunlight, with an ancient cratered surface that shows little evidence of resurfacing since formation. The standout feature is Wunda, a 131 km crater ringed with bright frost-like material around its rim, sitting near the moon's equator. The cause of Umbriel's overall dark colour is unknown; one hypothesis ties it to dust from Uranus's irregular outer moons sweeping across the inner system.
satellites/umbriel.json.surface_composition: Water-ice + carbonaceous-tinted regolith; dark, heavily-cratered surface — the least reflective of Uranus's major moons. Striking exception: the bright Wunda crater near the equator.

science_sections.why: Umbriel orbits Uranus at 266,000 km — its orbital plane is tilted with the planet, so its seasons mirror the parent's extreme axial geometry.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Falcon Heavy lifts off. Free-return — no landing.

events.label: TMI BURN
events.note: Trans-Mars Injection: 3.61 km/s. Escape velocity achieved.

events.label: DAY 1 CHECK
events.note: First systems health check complete. All nominal.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: Mid-course correction 1: 35 m/s.

events.label: CRUISE
events.note: Outbound cruise. Earth growing distant.

events.label: COMMS GLITCH
events.note: Brief X-band signal dropout (8 s). DSN reacquired. Cause: thruster plume occlusion. No data lost.

events.label: MARS FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach: ~300 km altitude. Gravity assist initiates return.

events.label: RETURN TRAJECTORY
events.note: Free-return gravity assist complete. Spacecraft on Earth trajectory.

events.label: MID-COURSE 3
events.note: TCM-3: 22 m/s. Return trajectory corrected.

events.label: HALFWAY HOME
events.note: Past midpoint of return journey.

events.label: RE-ENTRY PREP
events.note: Final approach. Heat shield checks.

events.label: EARTH ARRIVAL
events.note: Atmospheric entry. Mission complete.

science/_landing.json.intro_heading: So you want to fly a rocket to Mars.
intro_paragraphs: Welcome. This is the part of Orrery where the buttons stop being magic. Every label in the HUD, every coloured contour in the porkchop, every burn marker on the trajectory — this section explains where it comes from. Read it like a comic book: the diagrams do most of the work, and every italicised term is a link you can chase as deep as you want.

We're going to build a rocket together. Not a literal one — Orrery is a simulator — but the same chain of decisions a real flight team makes, in the order they'd make them. By the end you'll know why launch windows happen every 26 months for Mars and every month for the Moon, why a free-return trajectory exists, and why thrust is the cheapest part of a mission and fuel is the entire fight.

chapters.heading: 1 — Gravity is the only physics that matters.
chapters.diagram_alt: An ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
chapters.diagram_caption: One body, one focus, one ellipse. That's the whole solar system.
paragraphs: Forget rockets for a second. Stand on the Earth, throw a baseball as hard as you can. It comes back down. Throw it harder, it lands farther. Throw it so hard that the ground curves away faster than the ball falls, and the ball misses the planet — forever. That's an [orbit](orbits/keplerian-orbit). Every spacecraft, every planet, every rock in the asteroid belt is doing this trick around something heavier.

An orbit is an ellipse. It has a [size](orbits/semi-major-axis), a [shape](orbits/eccentricity) (round vs. stretched), a [tilt](orbits/inclination), and a phase telling you where on the ellipse the spacecraft is right now ([true anomaly](orbits/true-anomaly)). Five numbers and you can predict the position of any object in the solar system, forever, without any other data. That's [Kepler's three laws](orbits/keplers-laws), written down in 1609 — they still work.

The single most useful equation you'll meet here is [vis-viva](orbits/vis-viva). Plug in your radius, your orbit's size, and out comes your speed. That's it. Earth at perihelion: 30.3 km/s. Earth at aphelion: 29.3 km/s. Same orbit, same energy, different speed.

chapters.heading: 2 — The rocket equation is the boss fight.
chapters.diagram_alt: Mass-ratio curve: ∆v rises logarithmically with how much fuel you burn.
chapters.diagram_caption: The cruel truth: doubling your ∆v means burning a lot more than 2× the fuel.
paragraphs: Now: how do you change orbits? You burn fuel. [∆v](propulsion/dv-budget) ("delta-v") is the universal currency of spaceflight — the total velocity change a mission needs. Every move you make on a trajectory has a price tag in km/s.

And that price is brutal. The [Tsiolkovsky rocket equation](propulsion/tsiolkovsky) says ∆v scales with the logarithm of how much of your rocket is fuel. Want twice the ∆v? You don't carry twice the fuel — you carry exponentially more. This is why a Saturn V was 90% propellant. Most of the rocket is the fuel that lifts the fuel that lifts the fuel that lifts the spacecraft.

Two numbers fight this gravity tax. Thrust tells you how hard the engine pushes — that's the number nobody really cares about after launch. [Specific impulse](propulsion/specific-impulse) tells you how efficiently the engine pushes — and that's the one that matters. A chemical rocket gets ~450 seconds. An ion thruster gets 4,000+ — sips fuel for months and outperforms anything chemical for deep-space cruises.

Best magic trick of all: the [Oberth effect](propulsion/oberth-effect). Burning your engine when you're already moving fast (low and close to a planet) gives you way more bang for the same fuel. This is why every interplanetary mission does its big departure burn at perigee, hugging the Earth, going as fast as physics allows. Free energy from geometry.

chapters.heading: 3 — Once you're in orbit, you're halfway to anywhere.
chapters.diagram_alt: An ellipse tangent to Earth's orbit and Mars's orbit.
chapters.diagram_caption: Two burns, one ellipse. The cheapest way to change orbits.
paragraphs: Robert Heinlein wrote it: "Once you're in orbit, you're halfway to anywhere in the solar system." He wasn't kidding. Reaching low Earth orbit costs ~9.4 km/s of ∆v. Going from there to Mars costs another ~3.6 km/s. The hardest part is already behind you.

The cheapest interplanetary route is a [Hohmann transfer](transfers/hohmann-transfer): an ellipse that just barely kisses Earth's orbit at one end and the destination's orbit at the other. Two burns, no wasted fuel. To Mars it takes ~8.5 months. Slow, but optimal.

Want to go faster? Solve a [Lambert's problem](transfers/lambert-problem) — pick your departure date and your transit time, and Lambert tells you the unique [transfer ellipse](transfers/transfer-ellipse) that connects them. That's exactly what Orrery's [/plan](app:/plan) screen does, ten thousand times in parallel, to draw a porkchop plot.

Need to go even further? Steal speed from a planet. A [gravity assist](transfers/gravity-assist) uses a flyby to change your trajectory at zero fuel cost — Voyager 2 used four of them to reach Neptune. The whole solar system stitches together as [patched conics](transfers/patched-conics): a series of [conic-section](transfers/conic-sections) arcs handed off between gravitational neighbourhoods like batons in a relay race.

chapters.heading: 4 — Pick a launch window, or wait two years.
chapters.diagram_alt: The classic porkchop contour plot — departure date on x, time of flight on y.
chapters.diagram_caption: A porkchop. Each contour is constant ∆v; the lobe is when nature makes Mars cheap.
paragraphs: Earth and Mars don't sit still. Earth races around the Sun every 365 days, Mars every 687. Their relative geometry repeats only every ~26 months — and most of those months, the planets are too far apart, on the wrong sides of the Sun, to reach cheaply. Mission design starts with a calendar, not a rocket.

The [porkchop plot](porkchop/what-is-a-porkchop) is how engineers see this. Departure date along [one axis](porkchop/departure-axis), [flight time](porkchop/tof-axis) along the other, ∆v as a [colour heatmap](porkchop/dv-heatmap). Cheap zones appear as oval lobes — the launch windows. Outside the lobe: red, expensive, impossible-with-current-rockets. [Reading the contours](porkchop/contour-reading) is half the job of a flight dynamicist.

Two technical terms you'll see everywhere: [C3](propulsion/c3) is the launch energy your rocket needs to leave Earth's gravity well. [V∞](propulsion/v-infinity) ("v-infinity") is your speed relative to the destination at the moment you arrive. Both come straight out of the porkchop math.

chapters.heading: 5 — The flight is just five phases on repeat.
chapters.diagram_alt: Atmospheric entry, parachute deploy, retropropulsion, landing.
chapters.diagram_caption: Entry, descent, landing. Six minutes of pure terror.
paragraphs: Pretty much every interplanetary mission, from Voyager to Perseverance, runs the same script:

[Launch](mission-phases/launch) — get out of the atmosphere and into low Earth orbit. [Trans-X Injection](mission-phases/trans-x-injection) — a single hard burn at perigee that flings you onto the transfer ellipse to the Moon (TLI), Mars (TMI), Venus (TVI), or Jupiter (TJI). [Trajectory Correction Maneuvers](mission-phases/tcm) — tiny burns during cruise to fix dispersion errors. Usually 1–3 of them. [Orbit Insertion](mission-phases/orbit-insertion) — a braking burn at the destination to bend you into a captured orbit. [EDL](mission-phases/edl) — Entry, Descent, Landing — for the lander. Six minutes of supersonic atmospheric chaos.

Lunar missions sometimes detour through a [Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit](mission-phases/nrho) (Gateway will live in one), and crewed Apollo flights flew [free-return trajectories](transfers/free-return) — figure-8 paths that drop you back to Earth automatically if every engine on the spacecraft dies. Apollo 13 owes its life to this geometry.

chapters.heading: 6 — Distances and time, since none of this is Earth-sized.
chapters.diagram_alt: The astronomical unit, marked along Earth's orbital radius.
chapters.diagram_caption: One AU = one Earth-Sun distance. Mars is ~1.5 AU. Jupiter is ~5.2.
paragraphs: Three units pop up everywhere. The [astronomical unit](scales-time/au) (AU) is the average Earth-Sun distance — 150 million km. We measure the solar system in AU because kilometres get unwieldy fast. The [light-minute](scales-time/light-minute) tells you how long it takes a radio signal to reach a spacecraft. Mars: 4 to 24 minutes one-way. You can't joystick a rover from Earth. Everything important is autonomous.

The [J2000 epoch](scales-time/j2000) is the calendar zero every astrodynamicist uses. [Sidereal vs. synodic periods](scales-time/sidereal-synodic) explain why Mars windows recur every 26 months instead of every 23. The [ecliptic plane](scales-time/ecliptic-plane) is the flat disc the planets all (mostly) lie on. [Reference frames](scales-time/frames) are the coordinate systems mission control juggles between Earth-centred, Sun-centred, and body-centred views.

chapters.heading: 7 — Humans aren't built for this.
chapters.diagram_alt: A stylised astronaut floating in microgravity with bone/muscle/countermeasure indicator bars.
chapters.diagram_caption: Bone, muscle, vision, vestibular, immune — everything re-wires in microgravity, and not toward Earth.
paragraphs: Spend six months in orbit and you come back smaller, lighter, and shorter than you left. [Microgravity](life-in-space/microgravity-physiology) is the root cause: fluids redistribute headward, the postural muscles unload, the [bones](life-in-space/bone-density-loss) shed 1–2% of their mineral per month, the [vestibular system](life-in-space/vestibular-adaptation) gives up trying to find "down". The [counter-measures](life-in-space/muscle-atrophy) — two hours of resistive and aerobic exercise a day on ARED + the treadmill — slow it without solving it.

[Radiation](life-in-space/radiation-exposure) is the harder problem. The ISS gets ~200 mSv/year (vs 3 mSv background on Earth); deep space outside the magnetosphere is 600+ mSv/year, with no good shielding strategy yet. A Mars-class trip would put a crew member near career-limit cancer risk in a single round trip.

Then there's [EVA](life-in-space/eva-physiology) (a 6-hour endurance event in a 4.3 psi pure-oxygen suit) and [long-duration effects](life-in-space/long-duration-effects) like SANS — Space-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome — where 60% of long-flight crew develop measurable eye changes that don't fully reverse. These are the unsolved problems standing between humanity and Mars.

chapters.heading: 8 — Everything we know about the universe arrived as a photon.
chapters.diagram_alt: A space telescope aimed at a distant galaxy with a representative emission spectrum below.
chapters.diagram_caption: Telescope + filter + spectrograph + maths. Almost every fact about the cosmos was reconstructed from light.
paragraphs: [Space photography](observation/space-photography) is not what people think it is. There's no shutter clicking; every observatory image you've seen is a stack of long exposures through narrow-band filters, calibrated, registered, false-colour assigned. The hardware is a CCD or CMOS sensor — a grid of photon-counters — and the data is the count, not the picture. The picture is what humans make of the count.

[Adaptive optics](observation/adaptive-optics) defeats the atmosphere by measuring its distortion in real time and bending the mirror to cancel it. [Coronagraphs](observation/coronagraphs) block the central star to see the planets orbiting it. [Spectroscopy](observation/spectroscopy) reads a star's chemical composition from the absorption lines in its light. [Interferometry](observation/interferometry) stitches separate telescopes into one virtual aperture larger than any of them.

And the strangest objects those methods have found: [black holes](observation/black-holes) (real, mapped, shadow-imaged at the centre of two galaxies) and [wormholes](observation/wormholes) (pure mathematics, included so you know what to do with them when you see one in a film). The /fleet ↦ Observatory category has the actual machines — Hubble, JWST, Chandra, Spitzer, Kepler, TESS — each with its own gallery of what it saw.

science/_landing.json.tools_intro: That's the whole loop. You now know enough to read every label, contour, and HUD readout in the rest of the app. Here's where to put it to work:

tools.text: Spin the solar system. Watch Kepler's laws live. Click any planet for its orbital elements.
Pick a destination, pick a launch year, see the porkchop. The lobe is where Hohmann transfers hide.
Fly a real mission arc. The HUD shows ∆v, V∞, MET, distance to Earth. Every number is something you just learned.
36 real spacecraft, from Luna 9 to Artemis II. Each one's FLIGHT tab decomposes its actual ∆v budget across the phases above.
Ground truth. Where every Apollo, every rover, every active satellite actually sits.
The two inhabited orbital outposts, module by module.

science/_landing.json.closing: Below this story, the encyclopedia proper: six tabs, forty entries, every formula and every diagram in one place. Bookmark it. We'll be here when you need it.

science/exoplanets/_intro.json.headline: Exoplanets — the other solar systems.
paragraphs: For most of history the planets we knew fit on one page: the Sun's family. That changed in 1995, when the first world was confirmed around another Sun-like star. Today the count runs into the thousands, and the strangeness is the point — lava worlds hugging their stars, giant planets on wild tilted orbits, and small rocky worlds in the temperate zone where water could pool.

This tab is about how we find them — you cannot photograph most exoplanets, so we detect them by their fingerprints: a star's wobble, a periodic dimming, a gravitational flash. Then it turns to what we've learned: habitable zones, hot Jupiters, the seven chiming worlds of TRAPPIST-1, and the honest state of the question everyone asks — are we alone?
Every method section links into /explore, where you can drop into a real system on real orbits and watch the physics the article describes.

science/exoplanets/are-we-alone.json.title: Are We Alone?
science/exoplanets/are-we-alone.json.intro_sentence: Thousands of worlds later, the oldest question is closer to a test than ever — but honesty about what we do and don't know is the whole discipline.
narrative_101: The exoplanet count now runs into the thousands, and statistics say roughly every star hosts planets, with small rocky worlds in habitable zones numbering in the billions across the galaxy. The stage for life, at least, is vast.
That's what makes the silence loud. If habitable real estate is everywhere, where is everyone? — the question Enrico Fermi framed over lunch, still unanswered.
We have gone from 'are there other worlds?' — settled, yes — to 'are any of them alive?', a question we can finally start to test rather than only argue about.
body_paragraphs: The Drake equation frames the odds as a chain of factors — how many stars, how many with planets, how many habitable, how many that develop life, and so on. Exoplanet science has now pinned the first factors observationally: planets are common, and habitable-zone rocky worlds abundant. The later factors remain unknown.

The next step is empirical, not philosophical. Reading the atmospheres of temperate rocky worlds for biosignatures — patiently, with instruments and standards built to survive scrutiny — is how the question moves from the Drake equation's guesses toward a measurement.

The honest state of the art: no life beyond Earth has been detected, no biosignature confirmed. But for the first time, the tools to look are real — and that is the quiet revolution the exoplanet era has delivered.

We have not only listened but spoken. In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a three-minute pictogram toward the globular cluster M13, 25,000 light-years away, and in 1977 both Voyager spacecraft left Earth carrying the Golden Record — greetings, music, and images bolted to a probe now drifting between the stars. Both are gestures more than conversations, but they are humanity's first deliberate messages to whoever might be out there.

science/exoplanets/astrometry.json.title: Astrometry
science/exoplanets/astrometry.json.intro_sentence: Track a star's exact position on the sky and you can see it trace a tiny loop as an unseen planet swings it around their shared centre of mass.
narrative_101: Radial velocity catches the star moving toward and away from us. Astrometry catches the other component — the star's side-to-side wobble across the sky as a planet pulls it around.

The loop the star traces is fantastically small, measured in millionths of a degree, which is why astrometry was long the great near-miss of planet hunting: promised for decades, delivering little, because the precision simply wasn't there.

Space astrometry has changed that. ESA's Gaia mission has mapped the positions of nearly two billion stars with the precision needed to feel a giant planet's tug — and is beginning to harvest planets from those wobbles.
body_paragraphs: Astrometry measures a star's periodic displacement on the plane of the sky as it orbits the system's centre of mass. Unlike radial velocity, it senses the full orbit regardless of orientation, so it yields a true mass (not just a lower bound) and works well for planets on wide orbits, where the astrometric signal grows.

Historically it produced more retractions than planets — Barnard's Star is the classic cautionary tale, its famous 'planets' from 1960s astrometry all spurious. The signal is simply tiny, and instrumental drift easily fakes it.

Gaia's all-sky, high-precision astrometry is now delivering genuine detections and, crucially, true masses for planets found by other methods — closing a chapter that stayed open for most of a century.
science/exoplanets/astrometry.json.diagram_caption: The star traces a small loop on the sky as an unseen planet swings it around their common centre of mass.

science/exoplanets/biosignatures.json.title: Biosignatures
science/exoplanets/biosignatures.json.intro_sentence: The gases or features in a planet's light that could betray life — and why no single one is ever proof on its own.
narrative_101: If a distant world holds life, it might leave a chemical mark on its atmosphere — a gas that shouldn't be there without something making it. Oxygen on Earth is the classic example: it would vanish in a few million years if photosynthesis stopped replenishing it.
The trouble is that nature can fake it. Oxygen, methane, and other candidate 'biosignatures' all have non-living ways to accumulate, so any single detection is a clue, not a verdict.

The honest test is context and combination: the right gases together, out of chemical equilibrium, on a world where geology and starlight can't easily explain them. That's a high bar, and reaching it is the point.
body_paragraphs: A biosignature is an observable — a gas, a surface feature, a seasonal cycle — whose most plausible explanation is life. The strongest cases rely on chemical disequilibrium: combinations of gases (like oxygen with methane) that react away unless continuously resupplied, ideally alongside signs that abiotic sources are ruled out.

Every proposed biosignature has known false positives. Oxygen can build up from water photolysis on some worlds; methane has abundant geological sources. So the field emphasises multiple, mutually-reinforcing lines of evidence and careful modelling of the planet and its star before any claim.

No exoplanet biosignature has been confirmed. Detecting one would demand extraordinary evidence — which is exactly why the search is being built patiently, on instruments and standards designed to withstand the scrutiny such a claim would face.

science/exoplanets/direct-imaging.json.title: Direct Imaging
science/exoplanets/direct-imaging.json.intro_sentence: Blot out the overwhelming glare of the star and, for a lucky few planets, you can photograph the faint pinprick of light beside it.
narrative_101: Most exoplanets are found indirectly, by their effect on their star. Direct imaging is the exception — it captures actual photons from the planet itself, a genuine picture of another world.

The problem is contrast. A planet can be a billion times fainter than its star and sits right next to it, like spotting a firefly beside a lighthouse. So the technique hides the star behind a mask — a coronagraph inside the telescope, or a distant free-flying starshade — and lets the planet's light through.
It works best for the hardest planets to find by other means: young, hot, massive worlds on wide orbits, still glowing with the heat of their formation.
body_paragraphs: Direct imaging blocks or nulls the starlight (with a coronagraph or interferometer) to reveal planets and disks that would otherwise be lost in the glare. Because it detects the planet's own light, it uniquely enables spectroscopy of the world in isolation — a direct read on its temperature and atmosphere.

Its bias is the mirror image of the others: it favours large, self-luminous planets far from their stars (wide orbits ease the contrast problem, and youth keeps the planet hot and bright). Systems like HR 8799 — four giant planets imaged at once — and the sculpted debris ring of Fomalhaut are showcases.

The method drives the next generation of flagship instruments, whose goal is to image and take the spectrum of a rocky planet in a Sun-like star's habitable zone — and search its air for signs of life.
science/exoplanets/direct-imaging.json.diagram_caption: A coronagraph masks the star's glare so the faint, nearby planet becomes visible.

science/exoplanets/exoplanet-atmospheres.title: Reading Exoplanet Atmospheres
science/exoplanets/exoplanet-atmospheres.intro_sentence: During a transit, a sliver of starlight filters through a planet's air and carries the fingerprints of its gases back to us.
narrative_101: You can't land on an exoplanet, but you can taste its atmosphere from light-years away. When a planet transits, a thin ring of starlight passes through the atmosphere on its way to us, and each gas absorbs its own set of colours.

Split that light into a spectrum and the missing colours spell out what the air is made of — water, carbon dioxide, methane, sodium. This is transmission spectroscopy, and the James Webb Space Telescope was built for it.
So far JWST has detected carbon dioxide and other molecules on giant planets, and begun the far harder task of testing whether small rocky worlds around red dwarfs have any atmosphere at all.
body_paragraphs: Transmission spectroscopy measures how a planet's atmosphere absorbs starlight during transit, wavelength by wavelength, revealing its composition. Emission spectroscopy — catching the planet's own thermal glow just before it slips behind the star — adds temperature structure. Together they turn a transiting planet into a world with a measurable sky.

JWST has pushed the field from hot giants to the edge of rocky-world atmospheres: clear carbon-dioxide detections on gas planets, and sensitive searches around TRAPPIST-1 that so far suggest its innermost planets are largely airless. Red-dwarf flares make holding an atmosphere hard, and that verdict is exactly what these observations test.

The long-term goal is a rocky planet in a Sun-like star's habitable zone whose atmosphere can be searched for the gases life might produce — the technical bridge from finding worlds to characterising them.

science/exoplanets/fifty-one-pegasi.json.title: 51 Pegasi b: The First
science/exoplanets/fifty-one-pegasi.json.intro_sentence: In 1995 a giant planet was found skimming a Sun-like star every four days — the discovery that opened the exoplanet era and won a Nobel Prize.
narrative_101: For centuries other solar systems were pure speculation. That ended in October 1995, when Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced a planet around 51 Pegasi, an ordinary Sun-like star 50 light-years away.

The planet — 51 Pegasi b, informally Dimidium — was a shock: a Jupiter-mass world orbiting its star in just 4.2 days, far closer than any giant was thought able to form. The first exoplanet around a normal star was nothing anyone predicted.
It opened the floodgates. Within years, dozens more 'hot Jupiters' turned up, planet-formation theory grew a chapter on migration, and in 2019 Mayor and Queloz shared the Nobel Prize in Physics.
body_paragraphs: 51 Pegasi b was found by radial velocity: a clear ~4.2-day Doppler wobble revealing a planet of at least half Jupiter's mass orbiting perilously close to its star. It was the first confirmed planet around a main-sequence star other than the Sun.

The find was doubly important — it proved the radial-velocity technique worked, and it revealed a planet type (the hot Jupiter) that demanded orbital migration and rewrote formation theory. Its informal name, Dimidium, means 'half', for its minimum mass.
The 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics recognised Mayor and Queloz for the discovery — the moment the study of other worlds turned from philosophy into observational science.

science/exoplanets/habitable-zone.json.title: The Habitable Zone
science/exoplanets/habitable-zone.json.intro_sentence: The band of orbits around a star where a rocky planet could hold liquid water on its surface — not too hot, not too cold.
narrative_101: Water is liquid only over a narrow range of temperatures, and temperature falls off with distance from a star. So around every star there is a ring of orbits — the habitable zone — where an Earth-like planet could keep oceans rather than boiling or freezing them away.
The zone isn't fixed: a hot, bright star pushes it far out; a dim red dwarf pulls it in close. That's why habitable-zone planets around red dwarfs orbit in days, tucked right up against their stars.
'Habitable zone' is a hopeful shorthand, not a promise. A world there could still be an airless rock or a runaway greenhouse — location is necessary, not sufficient.
body_paragraphs: The circumstellar habitable zone is defined by stellar flux: the inner edge is where a runaway greenhouse would boil the oceans (Venus's fate), the outer edge where even a strong carbon-dioxide greenhouse can't stop global freezing (beyond Mars). Its distance scales with the square root of the star's luminosity, so it sits far from bright stars and close to faint ones.

Because small red dwarfs are by far the most common stars, most known habitable-zone planets orbit them — worlds like TOI-700 d and several of the TRAPPIST-1 planets. Their tight orbits bring complications: tidal locking and exposure to stellar flares that can strip an atmosphere.

The habitable zone is a first filter, not a verdict. Whether any of these worlds is actually habitable depends on things the zone can't tell us — an atmosphere, water, a magnetic field — which is why the frontier has moved to reading their air.
science/exoplanets/habitable-zone.json.diagram_caption: The habitable zone (shaded) — orbits where a rocky planet could hold liquid water; inward is too hot, outward too cold.

science/exoplanets/hot-jupiters.json.title: Hot Jupiters
science/exoplanets/hot-jupiters.json.intro_sentence: Giant planets orbiting scorchingly close to their stars — the surprise that greeted the very first exoplanet discoveries and rewrote how we think planets form.
narrative_101: The first exoplanets found around Sun-like stars were nothing like our own giants. Instead of a Jupiter parked far out in the cold, they were Jupiters roasting a few stellar radii from their stars, whipping around in days.

Nobody expected them. Gas giants were supposed to form far out, beyond the 'snow line' where ice can condense. A giant planet skimming its star violated the textbook — and forced a new idea: planets can migrate inward after they form.
Hot Jupiters are rare in absolute terms but easy to find — huge, close, and deeply transiting — so they dominated the early years and remain the best-studied exoplanets of all.
body_paragraphs: Hot Jupiters are gas giants on orbits of only a few days, with dayside temperatures often exceeding 1,000 degrees. Their existence implies large-scale orbital migration: they likely formed beyond the snow line and spiralled inward through interactions with the protoplanetary disk or with other bodies, ending up where no giant could have assembled in place.

Their size and proximity make them the workhorses of exoplanet atmosphere science. Inflated by their stars' heat, they produce deep transits and strong signals, and they were the first worlds to have their atmospheres, winds, and even escaping tails detected.
51 Pegasi b, the first planet found around a Sun-like star, is the archetype — and the reason planet-formation theory had to grow a chapter on migration.

science/exoplanets/microlensing.json.title: Gravitational Microlensing
science/exoplanets/microlensing.json.intro_sentence: When one star drifts precisely in front of another, its gravity magnifies the background star — and a planet adds a brief extra flash.
narrative_101: Gravity bends light. When a foreground star passes almost exactly in front of a far more distant one, it acts as a lens, briefly brightening the background star over days or weeks.

If the foreground star has a planet, the planet's own gravity adds a short, sharp spike on top of that smooth brightening — a blip lasting hours to a day that betrays a world you will never see directly.

Because it relies on a one-off chance alignment, each microlensing event happens once and never repeats. But the method reaches where others can't: cold planets far from their stars, and even free-floating worlds bound to no star at all.
body_paragraphs: Microlensing detects planets by the transient gravitational magnification they add to a chance alignment of two stars. It is uniquely sensitive to low-mass planets on wide, cool orbits — the region beyond the snow line that transits and radial velocity struggle to reach — and to rogue planets drifting alone through the galaxy.

The trade-off is that events are singular and unrepeatable, the host and planet are often too distant to study further, and the mass and separation come out somewhat degenerate. It is a statistical tool: it measures how common cold and free-floating planets are, more than it catalogues individual worlds.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will run a wide microlensing survey expected to find thousands of these otherwise-invisible planets, filling in the cold outer reaches of the exoplanet census.
science/exoplanets/microlensing.json.diagram_caption: A foreground star lenses a background one; an orbiting planet adds a brief secondary spike to the light curve.

science/exoplanets/orbital-resonance.jso.title: Orbital Resonance
science/exoplanets/orbital-resonance.jso.intro_sentence: When planets' orbital periods form simple whole-number ratios, their repeated alignments lock the system into a self-reinforcing rhythm.
narrative_101: If one planet orbits exactly twice for every once of its neighbour, the two line up in the same place over and over, and their gravitational nudges add up instead of averaging out. That's a resonance — a rhythmic lock between orbits.

TRAPPIST-1 is the showpiece: its seven planets sit in a near-unbroken chain of resonances, each period a tidy ratio of the next. Speed the system up and the alignments would ring out an actual musical scale.
Resonances are footprints of how a system formed — they arise when planets migrate inward together through the birth disk and catch each other in step.
body_paragraphs: An orbital resonance occurs when orbiting bodies exert regular, periodic gravitational influence on each other, usually because their periods are in a ratio of small integers. Resonances can stabilise a tightly packed system by keeping planets in a locked pattern, or destabilise one by pumping up eccentricities.

Chains of resonances, like TRAPPIST-1's, are strong evidence for convergent migration: planets forming farther out and drifting inward through the gas disk, becoming trapped in successive resonances as they go. The delicate arrangement also makes the planets' mutual tugs measurable as transit-timing variations, which is how their masses were weighed.
Resonance is a bridge between a system's present rhythm and its deep past — the orbits still carry the memory of how they assembled.
science/exoplanets/orbital-resonance.jso.diagram_caption: Planets in near-integer period ratios line up repeatedly, so their gravitational tugs reinforce.

science/exoplanets/planet-formation.json.title: Formation & Migration
science/exoplanets/planet-formation.json.intro_sentence: Planets condense from a disk of gas and dust around a young star — and often don't stay where they were born.
narrative_101: A new star is wrapped in a spinning disk of gas and dust. Grains stick into pebbles, pebbles into boulders, boulders into planet-sized bodies — the whole planetary system assembling from the leftovers of the star's own birth.
Where a planet forms depends on temperature: rock and metal condense close in, ice only beyond the 'snow line'. That's why the Solar System has small rocky worlds inside and giants outside.

But the exoplanet zoo — hot Jupiters, resonant chains — proved that planets migrate. They exchange momentum with the disk and with each other and can spiral far from where they were born, scrambling the tidy picture.
body_paragraphs: The nebular model builds planets by core accretion in a protoplanetary disk: dust coagulates into planetesimals, which merge into cores; a core beyond the snow line that grows fast enough can capture a massive gas envelope and become a giant before the disk disperses.

Migration reshuffles the result. Gravitational torques between a planet and the disk gas can drive large radial drift, delivering hot Jupiters to their scorching orbits and sweeping smaller planets into resonant chains. Later scattering between planets can tilt and stretch orbits further.

Exoplanet demographics — the abundance of close-in giants, the ubiquity of super-Earths, the resonant multis — are the observational constraints that any formation-and-migration theory now has to reproduce.

science/exoplanets/proxima-system.json.title: Proxima Centauri: The Nearest Planets
science/exoplanets/proxima-system.json.intro_sentence: Around the closest star to the Sun orbits a roughly Earth-mass planet in the habitable zone — the nearest potentially habitable world, 4.24 light-years away.
narrative_101: The nearest star to the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is a small red dwarf just 4.24 light-years away — and in 2016 astronomers found a roughly Earth-mass planet, Proxima b, orbiting it in its habitable zone.

It is the closest potentially habitable world we know of, which makes it the natural first target for any dream of reaching another star. The Breakthrough Starshot project imagines gram-scale light-sail probes crossing to it within a human lifetime.
The catch is the star itself: Proxima flares violently, and its habitable-zone planet — likely tidally locked — sits close enough to take the brunt, a serious threat to any atmosphere or life.
body_paragraphs: Proxima Centauri b was detected by radial velocity: a ~11-day signal implying a planet of at least about 1.1 Earth masses in the temperate zone of the M5.5 dwarf. A second, far lighter planet, Proxima d, was confirmed in the early 2020s on a tighter orbit — one of the lowest-mass planets known.

Proximity is the whole story. At 4.24 light-years the system anchors interstellar thought experiments, from Breakthrough Starshot's light sails to generations of science fiction, and is a priority target for future direct-imaging searches.

Habitability is genuinely uncertain. Red-dwarf flares, tidal locking, and the difficulty of confirming an atmosphere from Earth all keep Proxima b in the tantalising-but-unproven column — the nearest test case for whether red-dwarf worlds can be alive.

science/exoplanets/radial-velocity.json.title: The Radial-Velocity Method
science/exoplanets/radial-velocity.json.intro_sentence: A planet's gravity tugs its star into a tiny to-and-fro wobble; a spectrograph reads that motion as a Doppler shift in starlight.
narrative_101: A planet doesn't just orbit its star — the two swing around their shared centre of mass, so the star traces a small circle of its own. From our vantage that shows up as the star moving slightly toward us, then slightly away, over and over.

That approach-and-recede shifts the star's spectral lines blue then red — the same Doppler effect that raises and lowers a passing siren's pitch. Measure the shift precisely enough and the planet reveals itself, even though you never see it.
The wobble is minute: Jupiter tugs the Sun at about 12 metres per second, Earth at barely 9 centimetres per second. Reaching those speeds is a decades-long instrument story that is still unfolding.
body_paragraphs: Radial velocity was the first method to deliver, confirming 51 Pegasi b in 1995 and dominating the early exoplanet count. It measures the line-of-sight speed of the star from Doppler shifts in its spectrum; the amplitude of that speed (K) scales with the planet's mass and shrinks with orbital distance, so it favours massive planets on short orbits — the reason the first finds were 'hot Jupiters'.

Its great strength is mass: radial velocity yields the planet's minimum mass (m·sin i), the quantity that tells you whether a world is rocky, icy, or gas. Its limits are the unknown orbital inclination (only a lower bound on mass without a transit) and the wall set by the star's own surface churning, which mimics a wobble and currently hides true Earth-analogue signals.

Modern spectrographs like ESPRESSO reach sub-metre-per-second precision, enough to detect the sub-Earth worlds recently found around Barnard's Star. Paired with a transit, radial velocity turns a size into a density — and a density into a guess at what a planet is made of.
science/exoplanets/radial-velocity.json.formula_caption: The velocity semi-amplitude K grows with planet mass and shrinks with orbital period.
science/exoplanets/radial-velocity.json.diagram_caption: Star and planet orbit their common centre of mass; the star's line-of-sight motion shifts its spectrum blue then red.

science/exoplanets/super-earths-sub-nept.title: Super-Earths & Sub-Neptunes
science/exoplanets/super-earths-sub-nept.intro_sentence: The galaxy's most common planets are sizes the Solar System skipped entirely — bigger than Earth, smaller than Neptune.
narrative_101: Our own system has a gap: nothing between Earth and Neptune, a factor of nearly four in size with no members. The galaxy, it turns out, loves that gap — planets in it are the single most common kind we've found.

They come in two flavours that blur together: rocky 'super-Earths' up to about 1.5 times Earth's size, and gas-shrouded 'sub-Neptunes' above roughly twice Earth's size. In between sits a real scarcity — the 'radius valley' — that hints at how these worlds lose or keep their atmospheres.
Because we have no local example, these worlds are genuinely alien territory: we're still learning what they're made of and whether any could be habitable.
body_paragraphs: Statistically, super-Earths and sub-Neptunes are the most abundant planets in the galaxy, yet the Solar System contains none. The 'radius valley' — a dip in the number of planets around 1.5–2 Earth radii — appears to divide bare rocky cores from worlds that have held onto a thick hydrogen-helium or steam envelope.

The dividing line is likely set by atmospheric escape: close-in planets can have their light envelopes stripped by stellar radiation, leaving a rocky super-Earth, while those that keep the envelope read as larger, lower-density sub-Neptunes.

Mass-and-radius measurements from paired transit and radial-velocity data — and increasingly atmospheric spectra from JWST — are what let us sort one from the other and probe a class of planet Earth has no cousin to.

science/exoplanets/tidal-locking.json.title: Tidal Locking
science/exoplanets/tidal-locking.json.intro_sentence: Planets orbiting close to small stars often keep one face turned toward the star forever — permanent day on one side, permanent night on the other.
narrative_101: The Moon does it to Earth: it keeps one face toward us always, because tides have synchronised its spin to its orbit. The same thing happens to planets that hug their stars.

For a rocky world in the habitable zone of a red dwarf — orbiting in days, tucked in close — tidal locking is almost inevitable. One hemisphere bakes in endless daylight; the other freezes in endless night; a ring of perpetual twilight runs between.

It sounds hostile, but it isn't necessarily fatal to life. A thick atmosphere or an ocean can carry heat around the planet and even out the extremes — one of the big open questions for red-dwarf habitability.
body_paragraphs: Tidal locking (spin-orbit synchronisation) arises when a star's tidal pull brakes a close-in planet's rotation until its day equals its year. Because the effect strengthens sharply with proximity, essentially every rocky planet in a red dwarf's habitable zone is expected to be locked or in a related resonant spin state.

The consequence is an extreme, permanent temperature contrast between the substellar 'eye' and the antistellar night side. Whether that's habitable depends on heat transport: climate models show a sufficiently thick atmosphere or a global ocean can redistribute warmth and keep the terminator — or even much of the night side — temperate.
Since red dwarfs host most of the galaxy's habitable-zone real estate, the fate of tidally locked worlds like Proxima b is central to whether the most common habitable zones are actually habitable.

science/exoplanets/transit-timing.json.title: Transit-Timing Variations
science/exoplanets/transit-timing.json.intro_sentence: In a crowded system, planets tug on one another and arrive early or late; the drift in transit times reveals unseen worlds and weighs the ones we see.
narrative_101: A lone transiting planet arrives like clockwork — same interval, every orbit. But put several planets in one system and their mutual gravity nudges each other, so transits creep a little early or a little late in a repeating pattern.

Those few-minute drifts are a gravitational signature. Model them and you can weigh the planets from their tugs alone — no spectrograph needed — and sometimes infer a planet that never transits at all, felt only through its pull on the others.
This is how the seven small worlds of TRAPPIST-1 were weighed: too faint for radial velocity, their masses came from the way they hurry and delay each other across the star.
body_paragraphs: Transit-timing variations (TTVs) exploit the gravitational interactions between planets in the same system. A perfectly isolated planet transits with a constant period; interacting planets show periodic deviations whose amplitude and pattern encode the planets' masses and orbits.

TTVs shine exactly where radial velocity struggles — around faint, small stars whose Doppler wobble is buried in noise — and they can reveal non-transiting planets by their influence alone. They are most sensitive near orbital resonances, where repeated close encounters amplify the tugs.

The method's masses complement transit radii to give densities, which is why compact resonant systems like TRAPPIST-1 and Kepler's multi-planet chains are so well characterised despite orbiting dim stars.
science/exoplanets/transit-timing.json.diagram_caption: Mutual gravitational tugs make transits arrive early or late; the pattern of drift encodes the planets' masses.

science/exoplanets/transit.json.title: The Transit Method
science/exoplanets/transit.json.intro_sentence: When a planet crosses in front of its star, it blocks a sliver of light; that periodic dip in brightness betrays the planet and measures its size.
narrative_101: If a planet's orbit happens to be edge-on to us, once per orbit it passes directly between us and its star — a transit — and the star dims by a tiny, precise fraction while the planet is in front.

The depth of that dip is just the ratio of areas: a bigger planet blocks more light. An Earth crossing the Sun dims it by about one part in ten thousand; a Jupiter, by one percent. Catch the dips repeating on a clock and you have a planet's size and orbital period.

Only a small fraction of systems are lined up for us to see transits — but survey enough stars and the numbers win. That is exactly what NASA's Kepler and TESS missions did, from space, staring at hundreds of thousands of stars at once.
body_paragraphs: Transit photometry is the most productive method by far, responsible for the large majority of known exoplanets. It measures a planet's radius directly (from the fractional dip in starlight) and its orbital period (from the spacing of the dips); combined with a radial-velocity mass it yields a bulk density.

Its bias is geometric — it only catches the minority of systems whose orbits we see nearly edge-on — and it favours large planets on short periods, which transit more often and more deeply. False positives from eclipsing binaries and stellar activity mean transits are usually confirmed by a second method.

Beyond discovery, a transit is a door into a planet's air: during the crossing, a thin ring of starlight filters through the planet's atmosphere and imprints the fingerprints of its gases — the technique the James Webb Space Telescope now uses to sniff exoplanet skies.
science/exoplanets/transit.json.diagram_caption: As the planet crosses the star's disk, the measured brightness drops by the ratio of their areas, then recovers.

science/exoplanets/trappist-1-system.jso.title: TRAPPIST-1: Seven Earth-Sized Worlds
science/exoplanets/trappist-1-system.jso.intro_sentence: A dim red dwarf 40 light-years away hosts seven roughly Earth-sized planets — the richest compact system known, and a prime hunting ground for habitability.
narrative_101: In February 2017 NASA unveiled a system unlike any other: seven planets, all close to Earth's size, circling a single ultracool dwarf star barely larger than Jupiter, all packed closer to their star than Mercury is to the Sun.
Three or four of them fall in the habitable zone. The star is so dim that even those temperate worlds orbit in a matter of days, and the whole system would nest inside Mercury's orbit.

The seven move in a near-perfect chain of orbital resonances — a cosmic metronome — which let astronomers weigh them by their mutual tugs and made them the top small-planet targets for the James Webb Space Telescope.
body_paragraphs: TRAPPIST-1 (an M8 dwarf ~40 light-years away in Aquarius) hosts seven transiting planets, b through h, with radii from about 0.75 to 1.13 Earth. Discovered by ground-based transit surveys and Spitzer and announced in full in 2017, their masses came from transit-timing variations — the planets are far too faint for radial velocity.

The planets sit in a chain of first-order resonances, strong evidence they migrated inward together through the birth disk. Planets e, f, and g lie in the conservative habitable zone; all are likely tidally locked.

JWST is systematically probing their atmospheres. Early results point to the innermost worlds (b, c) being largely airless — the expected toll of red-dwarf flares — while the temperate outer planets remain the field's marquee test of whether the galaxy's most common habitable zones can hold air.

science/history/_intro.json.headline: History — how a few hundred years of physics put us in orbit.
paragraphs: Spaceflight didn't appear from nowhere. It rests on a stack of discoveries — Kepler's ellipses, Newton's gravity, Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation, Goddard's first liquid burn, Korolev's R-7 — each one assembled on the previous. This tab walks the milestones in chronological order, names the people who got there, and points back into the rest of /science where the maths lives.

We've cherry-picked six pivots: Kepler's ellipses, Newton's gravity, Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation, Goddard's first liquid burn, Korolev's R-7, and Apollo 11. Hundreds more deserve a place; future revisions will fill them in (Galileo's telescopes, Hohmann's transfer paper, Goddard's wife who took most of the photos, the Soviet engineers Korolev couldn't name in public, Ed White's spacewalk, von Kármán's altitude line). The story isn't owned by any one nation — every chapter has people you've never heard of who made it work.
Read it as a chain. Each step required the previous one. None were inevitable.

science/history/apollo-11-1969.json.title: Apollo 11 · July 20, 1969
science/history/apollo-11-1969.json.intro_sentence: Three astronauts, a Saturn V, and a moonshot deadline JFK set in 1961. Tranquillity Base, eight years later, on schedule.
narrative_101: On May 25, 1961, John F. Kennedy told Congress "this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth." Eight years later, almost to the month, Neil Armstrong stepped onto Mare Tranquillitatis. 400,000 people worked on Apollo at peak; the programme cost ~$25.4 billion total (1960–1973, nominal); NASA's budget peaked at ~4.4% of the federal budget in 1966.

Apollo 11: Commander Neil Armstrong, CMP Michael Collins, LMP Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin. Saturn V launch July 16; lunar orbit July 19; landing July 20 at 20:17 UTC; first step at 02:56 UTC July 21 (UTC; 22:56 EDT July 20 in the US). Splashdown July 24. 8 days, 3 hours, 18 minutes total.

The moon landing was watched live by an estimated 600 million people — about a fifth of humanity at the time. The "one small step" line was Armstrong's; it was unscripted (he later said he meant to say "one small step for a man" but the indefinite article got lost in transmission).
body_paragraphs: Saturn V was a 110-meter, three-stage liquid-fuel monster designed under Wernher von Braun (the German V-2 designer, brought to the US under Operation Paperclip in 1945). First stage: 5× F-1 engines, 7.6 million lbf thrust. Still the highest-thrust rocket to fly a fully successful crewed mission (SLS Block 1 and Starship exceed its raw liftoff thrust; nothing yet matched its crewed payload to TLI).

Trajectory: free-return loop, the "figure-8" Earth-Moon-Earth. If the lunar-orbit insertion burn failed, Apollo 11 would have looped around the Moon and returned to Earth on the same arc — built-in abort. Apollo 13 used exactly this property when its service module failed, looping behind the Moon and coming home.

Key personnel beyond the crew: George Mueller (NASA Apollo programme director), Christopher Kraft (Mission Control founder), Margaret Hamilton (Apollo Guidance Computer software lead — she ran the team that wrote the AGC code that ran on the LM during descent), Glynn Lunney + Gene Kranz + Cliff Charlesworth (flight directors).

Things-that-could-have-killed-them: AGC alarms 1201 and 1202 during descent (executive overflow — Hamilton's robust software design recovered automatically); manual landing because the auto-target was a boulder field (Armstrong landed with ~25 seconds of fuel left); the LM ascent engine had ONE chance to fire and was untested at full duration in flight.

Apollo flew six successful landings: 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17 (1969-1972). Apollo 13 missed the Moon (LOI cancelled), looped behind it, returned safely. 12 humans walked on the Moon; the last (Gene Cernan, Apollo 17) left on December 14, 1972.

science/history/goddard-liquid-rocket-19.title: Goddard's First Liquid-Fuel Rocket · 1926
science/history/goddard-liquid-rocket-19.intro_sentence: March 16, 1926: a 3-meter spindly contraption rises 12 meters into the Massachusetts sky. The first liquid-fuel rocket flight in history.
narrative_101: Robert Goddard was a physics professor at Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts, with a 1919 Smithsonian paper proposing rockets could reach the Moon — for which the New York Times mocked him in a 1920 editorial that claimed he didn't even understand high-school physics. (The Times retracted on July 17, 1969 — the day after Apollo 11 launched, as the spacecraft was en route to the Moon.)

On a snowy March 16, 1926, on his Aunt Effie Ward's farm in Auburn, Goddard launched a 4.4-pound, 10-foot rocket fueled by liquid oxygen and gasoline. It flew for 2.5 seconds, reached 41 feet altitude, and crashed in the cabbage field 184 feet downrange. His wife Esther Goddard photographed it. That short hop is the start of every modern rocket lineage.

Goddard was secretive — paranoid about competitors, refused most collaboration. His patents covered fundamentally everything: gimbaled engines, pumps, gyroscopic guidance, multi-stage configurations. Postwar Germans had read his patents; postwar Americans had to relearn most of his work because he hadn't shared it.
body_paragraphs: March 16, 1926 launch site: Aunt Effie Ward's farm, Auburn, Massachusetts. Vehicle: "Nell" — 10 ft tall, ~3 m long structure, weighing about 6 kg dry. Propellants: liquid oxygen + gasoline, regeneratively cooled, gimbaled nozzle.

Earlier solid-fuel rockets existed (Chinese fire-arrows from the 13th century onward, Congreve rockets in the Napoleonic wars), but liquid fuels were the door to spaceflight: higher specific impulse, controllable throttling, restartable.
Esther Goddard took most of the photographs. Her work is undercredited in standard histories — the iconic 1926 launch image is hers.

Goddard's later flights from Roswell, New Mexico (1930-1941), reached 1.7 mi altitude (Mar 1937) and 9000 ft (1941). Modest by modern standards but every key technology — gimbaling, pumps, gyros, parachute recovery — proved out on Goddard's hardware decades before mass-produced rocketry caught up.
Postwar acknowledgment: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland (1959) is named for him.

science/history/keplers-laws-1609.json.title: Kepler's Laws · 1609–1619
science/history/keplers-laws-1609.json.intro_sentence: Tycho Brahe's lifetime of naked-eye Mars data, distilled by Kepler into the three rules every orbit obeys.
narrative_101: Tycho Brahe spent ~20 years at the Uraniborg observatory on Hven measuring Mars's position with quadrants made of brass and oak — better-than-arcminute precision, all with naked eyes. He died in 1601 having published little of his planetary results.

Kepler inherited the Mars notebooks. He spent another decade trying to fit them to circles and failed. The break came when he tried an ellipse — Mars matched immediately. Out of that came three laws: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus; equal areas swept in equal time; period squared equals semi-major axis cubed.
Without those three laws, no spacecraft trajectory in this app would compute. Every porkchop cell, every transfer arc, every planet on /explore is a Keplerian solution.
body_paragraphs: Astronomia Nova (1609) published Laws 1 + 2 — the ellipse + equal-areas rules, derived from the Mars opposition data. Harmonices Mundi (1619) published Law 3 — period² ∝ semi-major axis³.

Kepler had no theoretical justification — the laws were empirical patterns extracted from data. Newton would supply the why 70 years later (gravity goes as 1/r²; bound orbits are conic sections; Law 3 falls out of energy conservation).

Brahe's contribution wasn't just data: he was a meticulous instrumentalist who pushed naked-eye measurement to its physical limit. Telescope-grade precision arrived only after Galileo's 1609 telescope — too late to overlap with Brahe's career.
Modern reanalysis: Kepler's Mars residuals are sub-arcminute. He nailed an ellipse with eccentricity 0.0934 from data that had irreducible measurement uncertainty of ~1 arcminute. The fit was real.
science/history/keplers-laws-1609.json.diagram_caption: Tycho's Mars positions (dots) versus Kepler's elliptical fit (curve). Sun at one focus.

science/history/newton-principia-1687.js.title: Newton's Principia · 1687
science/history/newton-principia-1687.js.intro_sentence: One book, three laws of motion, and the inverse-square law of gravity — the foundation everything spaceflight does still rests on.
narrative_101: By 1684 Halley was asking the right people what shape an orbit would take if the Sun's pull went as 1/r². Christopher Wren wagered a book of forty shillings that no-one could prove it; Hooke claimed a proof he didn't have. Halley asked Newton — Newton said "an ellipse" without hesitation, dug up the proof from years-old notes, and three years later published the Principia.

Three laws of motion (inertia, F = ma, action-reaction) plus the inverse-square gravity law (F = Gm₁m₂/r²) plus the calculus to do it all — one book, three years, no peer review. Halley paid the printing costs himself when the Royal Society ran out of money on a fish-anatomy book.

Out of those equations: Kepler's three laws derive cleanly. Tides, projectile motion, the precession of the equinoxes, the shape of the Earth — all consequences. Spaceflight 280 years later is straightforward Newtonian mechanics with engines added.
body_paragraphs: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica was published July 1687 in Latin. Three books: motion in a vacuum, motion through resisting media, the system of the world. The third book applies the laws to the actual cosmos and reproduces all of Kepler's data from first principles.

Calculus was Newton's invention specifically to do this. He called it "fluxions" — Leibniz independently invented essentially the same machinery in Germany around the same time, and the rivalry over priority lasted decades.

What Newton DIDN'T explain: WHY gravity follows 1/r². His own famous comment — added to the 1713 second edition: "Hypotheses non fingo" — "I feign no hypotheses." The mechanism would wait for Einstein in 1915.

Modern numerical orbit propagators run essentially Newton's equations with floating-point arithmetic. /fly's heliocentric arc, /plan's porkchop, every Keplerian solution — Newtonian gravity all the way down.
science/history/newton-principia-1687.js.formula_caption: Newton's law of universal gravitation. G ≈ 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

science/history/sputnik-1957.json.title: Sputnik 1 · October 4, 1957
