sun.json.name: The Sun
sun.json.fact: The Sun contains 99.86% of all mass in the solar system. Its gravity holds everything — from Mercury to the Oort Cloud — in orbit. Every second, it fuses 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that has sustained life on Earth for 4.5 billion years.
sun.json.bio: A 4.6-billion-year-old G-type main-sequence star, halfway through its 10-billion-year life. The Sun rotates differentially — its equator takes 25 days, its poles 35. In about 5 billion years it will exhaust its core hydrogen, expand into a red giant, and engulf the inner planets. The Sun's gravitational influence defines the heliosphere out to roughly 120 AU.

links.l: Standard Solar Model (Annual Review of Astronomy 2022)

science_sections.why: Every planet, moon-of-a-planet, comet, and human-made spacecraft orbits because the Sun's gravity sets the central potential — a Keplerian orbit IS an orbit around the Sun.
Kepler derived his three laws by trying to fit Tycho's Mars data to the Sun's gravity — his second law (equal areas) is what makes inner planets faster than outer ones.
The astronomical unit is by definition the mean Earth-Sun distance — every solar-system distance reads relative to this scale.
The Sun's equator and the ecliptic plane are tilted by only 7.25° — close enough that 'orbits in the ecliptic' is a fine first approximation for almost everything in the system.
All inertial reference frames in solar system mechanics are defined relative to the Sun's barycentre — the rest of the system is co-moving.

tiangong-modules/chinarm.json.name: Chinarm
tiangong-modules/chinarm.json.description: The station's primary manipulator—a 10-metre, seven-joint arm that walks hand-over-hand across Tianhe and the lab modules to capture cargo and reposition external payloads.
tiangong-modules/chinarm.json.function_detail: Berthing assistance for Tianzhou cargo, EVA support for crew, and external payload transfers; cooperates with Wentian's small experimental arm for fine-grained work.

tiangong-modules/mengtian.json.name: Mengtian (Dreaming of the Heavens)
tiangong-modules/mengtian.json.description: The second laboratory—completed the canonical T-shape silhouette in October 2022, two more solar wings, and a cargo-style external payload airlock that doesn't need a spacewalker to operate.
tiangong-modules/mengtian.json.function_detail: Microgravity physics, fluid mechanics, and combustion experiments; automated payload deployment via its small robotic transfer mechanism.

tiangong-modules/tianhe.json.name: Tianhe (Core Module)
tiangong-modules/tianhe.json.description: Launched April 2021 as the spine of the station—propulsion, power, life support, and the docking hub where Wentian and Mengtian were swung into the perpendicular T over the next eighteen months.
tiangong-modules/tianhe.json.function_detail: Crew habitat, command and data handling, station-keeping thrusters, and the central dock for arriving Shenzhou crew and Tianzhou cargo.

tiangong-modules/wentian.json.name: Wentian (Quest for the Heavens)
tiangong-modules/wentian.json.description: The first laboratory, berthed July 2022—two large solar wings, an external payload airlock, and a small experimental robotic arm bolted to its hull.
tiangong-modules/wentian.json.function_detail: Life-science research, EVA airlock for crew exits, and backup attitude control for Tianhe via redundant guidance systems.

tiangong-visitors/shenzhou.json.name: Shenzhou
tiangong-visitors/shenzhou.json.description: China's three-seat crew capsule—six-and-a-half-hour fast rendezvous from Jiuquan and a parachute landing on the Inner Mongolian grassland.
tiangong-visitors/shenzhou.json.function_detail: Tiangong crew rotation, lifeboat capability, and autonomous rendezvous and docking with manual override from the orbital module's controls.

tiangong-visitors/tianzhou.json.name: Tianzhou
tiangong-visitors/tianzhou.json.description: The pressurised cargo freighter, launched on Long March 7 from Wenchang—propellant, food, water, and experiment hardware delivered roughly every six months.
tiangong-visitors/tianzhou.json.function_detail: Tianhe propellant top-up, dry-cargo crew supplies, and on-orbit waste removal via destructive reentry over the South Pacific.

universe/exoplanets/51-peg-b.json.fact: The first planet found orbiting a Sun-like star — the world that opened the exoplanet era.
universe/exoplanets/51-peg-b.json.bio: 51 Pegasi b, informally named Dimidium, was discovered in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz — the first confirmed planet around a normal Sun-like star, a find that earned them the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. A 'hot Jupiter' skimming its star every four days, it stunned astronomers who never expected a giant planet so close in, and forced a rethink of how planetary systems form and migrate.

universe/exoplanets/alf-ari-b.json.fact: A giant planet candidate at Hamal — the Ram's star that once marked the spring equinox.
universe/exoplanets/alf-ari-b.json.bio: Hamal (Alpha Arietis), the brightest star of Aries, anchored the vernal equinox two thousand years ago and still lends its name to the zero-point of the sky. A planet nearly twice Jupiter’s mass has been inferred from the orange giant's motion, placing another world around one of the zodiac's oldest landmark stars.

universe/exoplanets/alf-tau-b.json.fact: A massive planet proposed at Aldebaran — the fiery eye of the Bull and a sci-fi waypoint.
universe/exoplanets/alf-tau-b.json.bio: Aldebaran, the orange-giant eye of Taurus, is one of science fiction's most name-dropped stars, from pulp adventures to film. A planet several times Jupiter's mass has been proposed around it from decades of subtle velocity signals, though the giant star's own pulsations make the detection debated — a reminder of how hard planets are to pin down around restless old suns.

universe/exoplanets/barnard-b.json.fact: A planet at Barnard's Star — the storied sci-fi sun that eluded planet-hunters for a century.
universe/exoplanets/barnard-b.json.bio: Barnard's Star, the second-nearest star system at six light-years, is a fixture of science fiction — the destination of the British Interplanetary Society's 1970s 'Project Daedalus' starship study and a waypoint in interstellar fiction from Robert Forward’s Rocheworld to the later Rama novels. After a century of claimed planets that all evaporated under scrutiny, Barnard b was finally confirmed in 2024: a sub-Earth far too hot for life, but real at last.

universe/exoplanets/barnard-c.json.fact: One of a compact family of sub-Earths recently found circling the storied Barnard's Star.
universe/exoplanets/barnard-c.json.bio: Barnard c is part of a tightly packed system of small, low-mass worlds confirmed around Barnard's Star in 2024–2025 with the ESPRESSO spectrograph. Each planet is a fraction of Earth's mass and orbits in just days, far too hot for life — but their discovery finally delivered real planets at a star that had frustrated hunters for a hundred years.

universe/exoplanets/barnard-d.json.fact: A sub-Earth in Barnard's Star's newly revealed inner system.
universe/exoplanets/barnard-d.json.bio: Barnard d is one of the diminutive worlds detected around Barnard's Star, a red dwarf just six light-years away. Weighing well under an Earth mass and orbiting close to its cool star, it helps make our second-nearest stellar neighbour a genuine planetary system rather than the empty sky once assumed.

universe/exoplanets/barnard-e.json.fact: The lightest of Barnard's Star's little worlds — near the edge of detectability.
universe/exoplanets/barnard-e.json.bio: Barnard e is the smallest planet found around Barnard's Star, only about a fifth of Earth's mass. Teasing such a feeble signal out of the star's motion pushed the ESPRESSO instrument to its limits, extending the roster of the nearest single star known to host planets.

universe/exoplanets/gj-273-b.json.fact: A habitable-zone super-Earth at Luyten's Star — and the target of a deliberate message from Earth.
universe/exoplanets/gj-273-b.json.bio: GJ 273 b, also called Luyten b, is a super-Earth in the temperate zone of Luyten's Star, only about 12 light-years away. In 2017–2018 the 'Sónar Calling GJ 273b' project beamed a coded radio message toward it from a radar in Norway — one of the few deliberate attempts to contact a specific nearby world, with any reply not due until the 2040s.

universe/exoplanets/gj-273-c.json.fact: A hot inner companion to Luyten's habitable-zone world.
universe/exoplanets/gj-273-c.json.bio: GJ 273 c is a small, hot planet orbiting Luyten's Star close in, interior to its more famous sibling GJ 273 b. Together they make Luyten's Star — a dim red dwarf near bright Procyon — one of the nearest multi-planet systems to the Sun.

universe/exoplanets/gj-411-b.json.fact: A hot super-Earth at Lalande 21185 — one of the nearest planet-hosting stars.
universe/exoplanets/gj-411-b.json.bio: GJ 411 b is a super-Earth whipping around Lalande 21185, a dim red dwarf about eight light-years away in the Great Bear and one of the closest stars to the Sun. First detected in 2017 and confirmed in 2020 from the star's tiny velocity wobble, it orbits far too close to be habitable, but its nearness makes the system a recurring waypoint in interstellar-travel fiction.

universe/exoplanets/hd-62509-b.json.fact: A giant planet circling Pollux — the first world found around a nearby giant star.
universe/exoplanets/hd-62509-b.json.bio: Pollux b (Beta Geminorum b) is a gas giant several times Jupiter's mass orbiting Pollux, the brighter of the mythological Twins and the nearest giant star to the Sun. Confirmed in 2006 from the star's slow wobble, it showed that even evolved giant stars — the Sun's own distant future — can keep massive planets in tow.

universe/exoplanets/hd-95735-c.json.fact: A second, cooler world orbiting nearby Lalande 21185.
universe/exoplanets/hd-95735-c.json.bio: A second planet around Lalande 21185, larger and farther out than GJ 411 b, was reported in the early 2020s from continued monitoring of the star. Together the planets make one of the Sun's nearest multi-planet systems — around a star already famous for its swift motion across our sky.

universe/exoplanets/proxima-cen-b.json.fact: The closest exoplanet to Earth — a roughly Earth-mass world in the habitable zone of the nearest star.
universe/exoplanets/proxima-cen-b.json.bio: Proxima Centauri b orbits the Sun's nearest neighbour just 4.24 light-years away, circling its cool red dwarf every 11 days within the zone where liquid water could exist. Its proximity made it the headline target of the Breakthrough Starshot project, which imagines gram-scale light-sail probes reaching it within a human lifetime — though the star's violent flares are a serious hazard to any atmosphere or life.

universe/exoplanets/proxima-cen-d.json.fact: A feather-light sub-Earth hugging the nearest star — one of the lowest-mass planets ever found.
universe/exoplanets/proxima-cen-d.json.bio: Proxima Centauri d is a tiny world, only about a quarter of Earth's mass, whirling around Proxima Centauri every five days far too close to be habitable. Confirmed in the 2020s, it sits near the very limit of what our instruments can detect, a testament to how precisely we can now weigh unseen planets by the wobble they induce in their star.

universe/exoplanets/toi-700-b.json.fact: The innermost world of TOI-700 — a rocky planet just smaller than Earth.
universe/exoplanets/toi-700-b.json.bio: TOI-700 b is a roughly Earth-sized rocky planet orbiting close to TOI-700, a red dwarf about 101 light-years away, completing a lap in only about ten days. It is the warm inner member of a system that NASA's TESS mission made famous for the temperate worlds farther out.

universe/exoplanets/toi-700-c.json.fact: A sub-Neptune in the middle of the TOI-700 system.
universe/exoplanets/toi-700-c.json.bio: TOI-700 c is a larger, likely gas-rich world between the system's rocky planets, too hot and puffy for habitability. It sits between the inner rocky planet b and the temperate, Earth-sized planets d and e that drew the world's attention to this red-dwarf system.

universe/exoplanets/toi-700-d.json.fact: TESS's first Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone — a landmark find.
universe/exoplanets/toi-700-d.json.bio: TOI-700 d, announced by NASA in 2020, was the first Earth-sized planet found in the habitable zone by the TESS mission. Orbiting a quiet red dwarf, it receives a gentle share of starlight that could allow liquid water, making it a benchmark case in the search for potentially habitable worlds close to home.

universe/exoplanets/toi-700-e.json.fact: A second Earth-sized world in TOI-700's habitable zone, found three years after the first.
universe/exoplanets/toi-700-e.json.bio: TOI-700 e, confirmed in 2023, is a rocky, roughly Earth-sized planet orbiting within the habitable zone just inside its sibling TOI-700 d. Finding two temperate Earth-sized worlds in one nearby system made TOI-700 an especially rich target for future studies of small-planet atmospheres.

universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-b.json.fact: The innermost of TRAPPIST-1's seven Earth-sized worlds — scorched and, JWST found, likely airless.
universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-b.json.bio: TRAPPIST-1 b is the closest planet to the ultracool dwarf star, baked far too hot for water. In 2023 it became one of the first rocky exoplanets probed for an atmosphere by the James Webb Space Telescope, which found little sign of a thick one — an early verdict in the long effort to learn whether any of these seven worlds can hold onto air.

universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-c.json.fact: The second of the seven — a Venus-sized world that Webb found nearly bare of atmosphere.
universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-c.json.bio: TRAPPIST-1 c is close in size to Venus but, unlike Venus, JWST observations in 2023 suggested it lacks a dense carbon-dioxide blanket. Its study is part of the system's central question: whether planets around small, flare-prone red dwarfs can keep atmospheres at all.

universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-d.json.fact: A small world at the warm inner edge of TRAPPIST-1's habitable zone.
universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-d.json.bio: TRAPPIST-1 d is among the smaller of the seven planets and sits just inside the zone where temperatures might allow liquid water. Like all its siblings it is thought to be tidally locked, keeping one face forever toward the dim red star and the other in perpetual night.

universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-e.json.fact: The most Earth-like of the seven — a rocky world squarely in the habitable zone.
universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-e.json.bio: TRAPPIST-1 e is widely considered the system's best hope for habitability: rocky, close to Earth's size, and receiving about as much warmth as Earth does. When the seven-planet system was unveiled by NASA in 2017 it captured the world's imagination, and TRAPPIST-1 e remains a headline target for atmospheric searches with JWST.

universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-f.json.fact: A habitable-zone world that could, in principle, hold oceans.
universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-f.json.bio: TRAPPIST-1 f orbits within the temperate zone of TRAPPIST-1 and is light enough to suggest a substantial share of water or ice. It is one of three planets — e, f, and g — that fall in the region where a suitable atmosphere might permit surface water.

universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-g.json.fact: The largest of the seven, at the cool outer edge of the habitable zone.
universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-g.json.bio: TRAPPIST-1 g is the biggest planet in the system and sits toward the outer boundary of the temperate zone, where any liquid water would need a strong greenhouse to survive. The seven planets circle their star in a delicate chain of orbital resonances, each period a near-whole-number ratio of its neighbour's.

universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-h.json.fact: The outermost and coldest of the seven Earth-sized worlds.
universe/exoplanets/trappist-1-h.json.bio: TRAPPIST-1 h is the farthest planet from the ultracool dwarf, likely frozen, completing the remarkable family of seven roughly Earth-sized worlds packed closer to their star than Mercury is to the Sun. All seven would fit comfortably inside the orbit of our innermost planet.

universe/named-stars/achernar.json.fact: The 'end of the river' — spinning so fast it is squashed into the sky's most flattened star.
universe/named-stars/achernar.json.bio: Achernar (Alpha Eridani) is a hot blue star about 139 light-years away marking the southern end of the celestial river Eridanus. It rotates near its break-up speed, bulging so strongly at the equator that its diameter there is roughly half again its polar diameter — the most oblate star known among the bright ones.
universe/named-stars/achernar.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the end of the river'. Lying deep in the southern sky, it was invisible to the classical Mediterranean astronomers and entered star charts only with the age of southern-hemisphere exploration.

universe/named-stars/acrux.json.fact: The brightest jewel of the Southern Cross — and the southernmost first-magnitude star.
universe/named-stars/acrux.json.bio: Acrux (Alpha Crucis) is a hot blue multiple system about 320 light-years away, the luminous foot of the Southern Cross. Its component stars are young and massive, blazing in blue-white light.
universe/named-stars/acrux.json.cultural: As the leading star of Crux, Acrux shares in the Southern Cross that appears on the national flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Papua New Guinea and Samoa. For cultures across the southern hemisphere the Cross is a central navigational and seasonal marker.

universe/named-stars/adhara.json.fact: The second star of the Great Dog — and once the brightest ultraviolet beacon in our sky.
universe/named-stars/adhara.json.bio: Adhara (Epsilon Canis Majoris) is a hot blue-white pair about 430 light-years away, the second-brightest star in Canis Major after Sirius. A few million years ago it passed much closer to the Sun and was then the brightest star in Earth's entire sky.
universe/named-stars/adhara.json.cultural: The traditional name comes from an Arabic term for 'the maidens'. Though outshone today by its neighbour Sirius, Adhara remains a powerful source of ultraviolet light illuminating the surrounding interstellar gas.

universe/named-stars/aldebaran.json.fact: The fiery orange 'eye of the bull' in Taurus — a giant star that only appears to sit among the Hyades cluster.
universe/named-stars/aldebaran.json.bio: Aldebaran (Alpha Tauri) is an orange giant about 65 light-years away. It lies in the foreground of the more distant Hyades cluster, a line-of-sight coincidence rather than true membership.
universe/named-stars/aldebaran.json.cultural: Aldebaran is one of the four 'Royal Stars' of ancient Persian astronomy. Its name means 'the follower', for the way it trails the Pleiades across the sky.

universe/named-stars/algol.json.fact: The 'Demon Star' — it winks every few days as an unseen companion eclipses it.
universe/named-stars/algol.json.bio: Algol (Beta Persei) is a multiple system about 90 light-years away and the prototype of the eclipsing binary stars. Every 2.87 days a dimmer companion passes in front of the bright star, dropping its light noticeably for a few hours before it recovers.
universe/named-stars/algol.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the ghoul', and Algol marks the severed head of Medusa held by Perseus. Cultures from the Arab world to ancient Egypt seem to have marked this star's strange, regular 'winking' with unease long before its cause was understood.

universe/named-stars/alhena.json.fact: The bright foot of the Twins, marking a brand on the sky.
universe/named-stars/alhena.json.bio: Alhena (Gamma Geminorum) is a blue-white subgiant about 109 light-years away, the third-brightest star in Gemini and set at the foot of the Twins near the edge of the Milky Way.
universe/named-stars/alhena.json.cultural: The name comes from an Arabic word for a brand or mark once made on the necks of camels. It sits close to the winter Milky Way, in the path the Sun, Moon and planets can occult.

universe/named-stars/alioth.json.fact: The brightest star of the Great Bear, first in the handle of the Big Dipper.
universe/named-stars/alioth.json.bio: Alioth (Epsilon Ursae Majoris) is a peculiar white star about 81 light-years away, the brightest in Ursa Major. Its spectrum shows odd, shifting chemical signatures tied to a strong magnetic field.
universe/named-stars/alioth.json.cultural: The name derives from Arabic. As the first star in the handle of the Big Dipper — or the tail of the Great Bear — Alioth is a fixture of northern navigation and one of the 57 stars used in celestial position-finding.

universe/named-stars/alkaid.json.fact: The star at the very tip of the Big Dipper's handle — the end of the Great Bear's tail.
universe/named-stars/alkaid.json.bio: Alkaid (Eta Ursae Majoris) is a hot blue main-sequence star about 104 light-years away, the last star in the handle of the Big Dipper. Unlike the five central Dipper stars, it does not share their common motion through space — it only happens to lie along the same line.
universe/named-stars/alkaid.json.cultural: Its name comes from an Arabic phrase, 'the leader of the mourners' — in that tradition the Dipper's bowl was a bier and the handle stars a procession of mourning daughters following behind.

universe/named-stars/almach.json.fact: One of the sky's loveliest double stars — a golden sun paired with a blue one.
universe/named-stars/almach.json.bio: Almach (Gamma Andromedae) is a multiple system about 350 light-years away, celebrated for the vivid colour contrast between its bright golden-orange giant and a bluish companion — itself a triple — making it a favourite target for small telescopes.
universe/named-stars/almach.json.cultural: The name derives from an Arabic term for a small desert cat or lynx. Almach marks the foot of the chained princess Andromeda, at the far end of the constellation from her head at Alpheratz.

universe/named-stars/alnair.json.fact: The bright eye of the Crane, a hot blue star of the deep south.
universe/named-stars/alnair.json.bio: Alnair (Alpha Gruis) is a hot blue-white star about 101 light-years away, the brightest in the modern constellation Grus, the Crane. It shines with a clean blue-white light in the southern sky.
universe/named-stars/alnair.json.cultural: Its name comes from an Arabic phrase, 'the bright one', inherited from an older constellation figure. Grus was formed by late-16th-century navigators charting the southern stars.

universe/named-stars/alnilam.json.fact: The central pearl of Orion's Belt — a blazing blue supergiant seen across vast distance.
universe/named-stars/alnilam.json.bio: Alnilam (Epsilon Orionis) is a blue supergiant more than a thousand light-years away, the middle and most distant of the three stars of Orion's Belt. Its enormous true luminosity lets it hold its own in the Belt despite that gulf of space.
universe/named-stars/alnilam.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the string of pearls'. The three Belt stars are among the most universally recognised in the sky, used as a pointer to Sirius and Aldebaran and woven into star-lore worldwide.

universe/named-stars/alnitak.json.fact: The eastern star of Orion's Belt — a blue supergiant beside the glowing Flame.
universe/named-stars/alnitak.json.bio: Alnitak (Zeta Orionis) is a hot blue supergiant system about 1,260 light-years away, the easternmost of the three Belt stars. Its fierce ultraviolet light illuminates the nearby Flame Nebula, and the famous Horsehead is silhouetted close by.
universe/named-stars/alnitak.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the girdle' or 'belt'. As one of the three Belt stars it shares in the near-universal recognition of Orion across human cultures.

universe/named-stars/alphard.json.fact: 'The solitary one' — a lone orange giant in a wide, empty stretch of sky.
universe/named-stars/alphard.json.bio: Alphard (Alpha Hydrae) is an orange giant about 180 light-years away, by far the brightest star in the sprawling constellation Hydra, the Water Snake — and conspicuously alone in an otherwise dim region.
universe/named-stars/alphard.json.cultural: The Arabic name means 'the solitary one', chosen precisely because it has no bright neighbours. That isolation made it a clear and reliable marker in an otherwise faint part of the sky.

universe/named-stars/alphecca.json.fact: The jewel of the Northern Crown — a bright star set in a delicate arc.
universe/named-stars/alphecca.json.bio: Alphecca (Alpha Coronae Borealis), also called Gemma, is a white star about 75 light-years away, the brightest in Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown. It is a faint eclipsing binary and, like Vega and Fomalhaut, is girdled by a disk of dust.
universe/named-stars/alphecca.json.cultural: 'Alphecca' comes from the Arabic for 'the broken one' — the broken ring of stars forming the crown — while the alternative 'Gemma' is Latin for 'jewel'. The small arc of Corona Borealis has been seen as a crown or a broken dish across many cultures.

universe/named-stars/alpheratz.json.fact: The shared corner of two figures — the head of Andromeda and a corner of Pegasus's Great Square.
universe/named-stars/alpheratz.json.bio: Alpheratz (Alpha Andromedae) is a blue-white star about 97 light-years away with an unusual mercury-manganese chemical peculiarity. It marks the head of Andromeda while also serving as the north-eastern corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.
universe/named-stars/alpheratz.json.cultural: The name derives from the Arabic for 'the navel of the mare', from a time when the star was counted as part of Pegasus. It bridges the myth of the chained princess Andromeda and the winged horse beside her.

universe/named-stars/altair.json.fact: The swift-spinning eye of the Eagle — rotating so fast it bulges into a flattened, egg-like shape.
universe/named-stars/altair.json.bio: Altair (Alpha Aquilae) is a hot white star about 17 light-years away, one of the closest naked-eye stars. It spins near its break-up speed — a full rotation in about nine hours — which flattens it markedly and makes its poles hotter and brighter than its equator. Interferometry has directly imaged this distorted, gravity-darkened surface.
universe/named-stars/altair.json.cultural: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-nasr al-ta'ir', the 'flying eagle'. Altair marks one corner of the Summer Triangle with Vega and Deneb, and in Chinese lore it is the cowherd Niulang, separated from the weaver Zhinu (Vega) by the Silver River of the Milky Way.

universe/named-stars/antares.json.fact: The red heart of the Scorpion — a vast red supergiant whose ruddy colour earned it the name 'rival of Mars'.
universe/named-stars/antares.json.bio: Antares (Alpha Scorpii) is a red supergiant roughly 550 light-years away, hundreds of times the Sun's diameter. Like Betelgeuse it is destined to end as a supernova.
universe/named-stars/antares.json.cultural: The Greek name means 'rival of Ares (Mars)', for its Mars-like hue. Many cultures place it at the heart or sting of a great scorpion or serpent along the Milky Way.

universe/named-stars/arcturus.json.fact: The brightest star of the northern sky's Boötes — an ageing orange giant racing through the galaxy on an unusual orbit.
universe/named-stars/arcturus.json.bio: Arcturus (Alpha Boötis) is an orange giant just 37 light-years away. It belongs to an older population of stars moving steeply relative to the galactic disc, giving it a large proper motion.
universe/named-stars/arcturus.json.cultural: In Hawaiian tradition Arcturus is Hōkūleʻa, the 'Star of Gladness' — the zenith star of Hawaii and a key wayfinding star for Polynesian voyagers, later lending its name to the famous voyaging canoe.

universe/named-stars/atria.json.fact: The apex of the Southern Triangle — an orange giant marking the deep south.
universe/named-stars/atria.json.bio: Atria (Alpha Trianguli Australis) is an orange giant roughly 390 light-years away, the brightest star of Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle.
universe/named-stars/atria.json.cultural: Its name is simply a contraction of its Bayer designation, 'Alpha Trianguli Australis'. The Southern Triangle was among the constellations introduced by the navigators who charted the far-southern sky in the late 16th century.

universe/named-stars/avior.json.fact: A giant of the Keel and a corner of the 'False Cross' — with a name coined in the age of flight.
universe/named-stars/avior.json.bio: Avior (Epsilon Carinae) is a system about 600 light-years away pairing an orange giant with a hot blue companion. It sits in Carina, forming one corner of the False Cross that is often mistaken for the true Southern Cross.
universe/named-stars/avior.json.cultural: Avior is one of the few star names with no ancient roots — it was assigned in the 1930s for a British air-navigation almanac, when unnamed but bright southern stars needed labels for aviators and sailors.

universe/named-stars/barnards-star.json.fact: A dim red dwarf just 6 light-years away — famous for sweeping across our sky faster than any other star.
universe/named-stars/barnards-star.json.bio: Barnard's Star has the largest known proper motion of any star, crossing an apparent Moon's-width of sky roughly every 180 years — earning it the nickname 'Barnard's Runaway Star'. It is an ancient, low-mass red dwarf.
universe/named-stars/barnards-star.json.cultural: Its closeness and motion made it a long-running target in the search for nearby planets, and a staple destination in interstellar-travel fiction and early starship studies like Project Daedalus.

universe/named-stars/bellatrix.json.fact: The 'female warrior' — the hot blue star at Orion's shoulder.
universe/named-stars/bellatrix.json.bio: Bellatrix (Gamma Orionis) is a hot blue giant roughly 250 light-years away, marking the left shoulder of Orion the Hunter. It is one of the hotter, bluer naked-eye stars in the constellation.
universe/named-stars/bellatrix.json.cultural: The Latin name means 'female warrior' or 'Amazon star'. It has long been one of the recognisable corners of the Orion figure used to find the way around the northern winter sky.

universe/named-stars/betelgeuse.json.fact: A colossal red supergiant marking Orion's shoulder — so large it would swallow the inner planets if placed at the Sun.
universe/named-stars/betelgeuse.json.bio: Betelgeuse (Alpha Orionis) is a semiregular variable near the end of its life. Estimates place it several hundred light-years away with large uncertainty. It will one day end as a supernova — briefly rivalling the Moon in our sky.
universe/named-stars/betelgeuse.json.cultural: Its dramatic dimming in 2019–2020 (a dust cloud, not imminent collapse) drew worldwide attention. The name descends from Arabic, and the star features across countless sky-lore traditions as a shoulder or hand of the hunter.

universe/named-stars/canopus.json.fact: The sky's second-brightest star — a distant beacon so steady that spacecraft steer by it.
universe/named-stars/canopus.json.bio: Canopus (Alpha Carinae) is a rare yellow-white bright giant roughly 310 light-years away, intrinsically thousands of times more luminous than the Sun. Its brilliance and position far from the ecliptic make it an ideal fixed reference — Mariner and later probes carried 'Canopus star trackers' to hold their bearings in deep space.
universe/named-stars/canopus.json.cultural: Often linked to a helmsman of the Greek fleet at Troy, Canopus is 'Agastya' in Indian tradition — a revered sage of the southern sky. Too far south for much of Europe, it was a prized season- and latitude-marker for navigators of the southern seas.

universe/named-stars/capella.json.fact: The 'little she-goat' of the charioteer — a golden point that is secretly four stars.
universe/named-stars/capella.json.bio: Capella (Alpha Aurigae) is the brightest star in Auriga and the sixth-brightest in the sky, about 43 light-years away. Though it looks like one yellow star resembling the Sun, it is really two giant G-type stars orbiting closely, accompanied by a pair of faint red dwarfs.
universe/named-stars/capella.json.cultural: Its Latin name means 'little she-goat' — the goat carried on the shoulder of Auriga the Charioteer, with the nearby 'Kids' at her side. As one of the northernmost bright stars, it was a familiar winter-evening marker across Europe and the Near East.

universe/named-stars/castor.json.fact: The mortal Twin — a single point to the eye that is really six stars bound together.
universe/named-stars/castor.json.bio: Castor (Alpha Geminorum) lies about 51 light-years away and is one of the most remarkable multiple systems in the sky: three pairs of stars — two bright white A-type binaries and a faint red-dwarf pair — all gravitationally bound, six suns in one 'star'.
universe/named-stars/castor.json.cultural: Castor is the mortal horseman of the Dioscuri, twin brother of Pollux in Greek and Roman myth. Though labelled 'Alpha', it is usually slightly fainter than its brother Pollux beside it.

universe/named-stars/deneb.json.fact: The Swan's tail — one of the most luminous stars the eye can see, shining from far across the galaxy.
universe/named-stars/deneb.json.bio: Deneb (Alpha Cygni) is a blue-white supergiant so distant — likely well over a thousand light-years — that its brilliance in our sky implies a true luminosity tens of thousands of times the Sun's, among the most powerful stars visible without a telescope.
universe/named-stars/deneb.json.cultural: The name comes from the Arabic for 'tail', marking the tail of Cygnus the Swan. Deneb anchors the Summer Triangle with Vega and Altair and rides the length of the Milky Way's northern stream.

universe/named-stars/denebola.json.fact: The 'tail of the Lion' — a fast-spinning young white star with a disk of dust.
universe/named-stars/denebola.json.bio: Denebola (Beta Leonis) is a white main-sequence star just 36 light-years away, marking the tail of Leo the Lion. It rotates quickly and is surrounded by a disk of cool debris left over from planet-building.
universe/named-stars/denebola.json.cultural: The name comes from the Arabic 'dhanab al-asad', 'the tail of the lion'. In older astrology it was considered a star of ill fortune, in contrast to the regal Regulus at the Lion's heart.

universe/named-stars/diphda.json.fact: The 'second frog' — an orange giant that outshines its own constellation's alpha star.
universe/named-stars/diphda.json.bio: Diphda (Beta Ceti), also called Deneb Kaitos, is an orange giant about 96 light-years away. Though lettered 'Beta', it is the brightest star in Cetus, the Sea Monster, outshining the constellation's Alpha, Menkar.
universe/named-stars/diphda.json.cultural: The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the second frog' — distant Fomalhaut being the 'first frog'. Its alternative name, Deneb Kaitos, marks the tail of the great sea beast of the watery region of the sky.

universe/named-stars/dubhe.json.fact: One of the two Pointer stars that guide the eye from the Dipper to the Pole Star.
universe/named-stars/dubhe.json.bio: Dubhe (Alpha Ursae Majoris) is an orange giant about 123 light-years away, one of the two 'Pointers' at the front of the bowl of the Big Dipper. A line drawn through Dubhe and its neighbour Merak points almost exactly at Polaris.
universe/named-stars/dubhe.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the bear'. The Pointers have guided travellers to the North Star for millennia, making Dubhe one of the most practically useful stars in the northern sky.

universe/named-stars/elnath.json.fact: The butting horn-tip of the Bull, on the border it once shared with the Charioteer.
universe/named-stars/elnath.json.bio: Elnath (Beta Tauri) is a blue-white giant about 130 light-years away, marking the tip of the northern horn of Taurus the Bull. It sits so close to Auriga that it was historically counted as a star shared between the two constellations.
universe/named-stars/elnath.json.cultural: The name comes from the Arabic for 'the butting' — the point of the Bull's horn. Its position on the edge of the Milky Way made it a useful signpost between Taurus and Auriga.

universe/named-stars/fomalhaut.json.fact: The 'lonely star' of the southern autumn sky — a young star girdled by a sharp-edged ring of debris.
universe/named-stars/fomalhaut.json.bio: Fomalhaut (Alpha Piscis Austrini) is a hot white star about 25 light-years away, one of the brightest in the sky and conspicuously isolated from other bright stars. It is encircled by a striking dusty debris ring, sculpted by unseen gravity — one of the first such rings ever imaged in visible light.
universe/named-stars/fomalhaut.json.cultural: Its name comes from the Arabic for 'mouth of the [southern] fish'. One of the four ancient Persian 'Royal Stars', Fomalhaut was a marker of the season and a waypoint for navigators of the southern horizon.

universe/named-stars/gacrux.json.fact: The red top of the Southern Cross — the nearest red giant to the Sun.
universe/named-stars/gacrux.json.bio: Gacrux (Gamma Crucis) is a cool red giant about 89 light-years away, the closest red giant to our Solar System. Its warm orange light sits at the head of the Southern Cross, a vivid contrast to the hot blue stars that form the rest of the figure.
universe/named-stars/gacrux.json.cultural: Its name is a modern contraction of 'Gamma Crucis'. As part of Crux it features in southern-hemisphere navigation and appears, with its companions, on several national flags of the south.

universe/named-stars/hadar.json.fact: A blue giant and one of the two bright 'Pointers' aiming at the Southern Cross.
universe/named-stars/hadar.json.bio: Hadar (Beta Centauri), also called Agena, is a hot blue system of massive stars around 390 light-years away, the eleventh-brightest in the sky. Together with nearby Rigil Kentaurus it forms the Southern Pointers that lead the eye to the Southern Cross.
universe/named-stars/hadar.json.cultural: Its traditional name derives from Arabic. As a brilliant southern beacon it has long served navigators below the equator, and it appears alongside the Cross in the sky-lore of many southern cultures.

universe/named-stars/hamal.json.fact: The Ram's brightest star — once the marker of the spring equinox.
universe/named-stars/hamal.json.bio: Hamal (Alpha Arietis) is an orange giant about 66 light-years away, the brightest star in Aries the Ram, and it hosts a giant planet detected from its motion.
universe/named-stars/hamal.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the lamb' or 'ram'. Around two thousand years ago the Sun crossed the vernal equinox near Hamal, so the 'First Point of Aries' — still the zero of celestial longitude — carries the Ram's name even though precession has since moved the crossing into Pisces.

universe/named-stars/kaus-australis.json.fact: The 'southern bow' of the Archer, brightest star aiming toward the galaxy's heart.
universe/named-stars/kaus-australis.json.bio: Kaus Australis (Epsilon Sagittarii) is a blue-white star about 143 light-years away, the brightest in Sagittarius. It forms the lower part of the Archer's drawn bow, which points across the rich star clouds toward the centre of the Milky Way.
universe/named-stars/kaus-australis.json.cultural: 'Kaus' comes from the Arabic for 'bow', with the Latin 'australis' for 'southern'. The bow-and-arrow of Sagittarius aims at the heart of the galaxy, a direction dense with the Milky Way's brightest clouds.

universe/named-stars/lalande-21185.json.fact: A dim red dwarf in the Great Bear — one of the closest stars to the Sun, yet invisible to the eye.
universe/named-stars/lalande-21185.json.bio: Lalande 21185 is a red dwarf about 8.3 light-years away in Ursa Major, among the nearest star systems to the Sun. Despite its nearness it is far too faint to see without a telescope, and it drifts across the sky with a large proper motion. Careful measurements point to a family of planets orbiting it.
universe/named-stars/lalande-21185.json.cultural: It carries no ancient name — only its entry number in the 18th-century star catalogue of the French astronomer Joseph Jérôme de Lalande. Such faint nearby stars became important only once astronomers began measuring stellar distances and motions.

universe/named-stars/luytens-star.json.fact: A nearby red dwarf with a planet — and a target of a deliberate message to the stars.
universe/named-stars/luytens-star.json.bio: Luyten's Star is a red dwarf about 12.4 light-years away in Canis Minor, not far in our sky from bright Procyon. It hosts a planetary system including a super-Earth in its habitable zone — a world so nearby that it has been chosen as a target for interstellar radio messages sent from Earth.
universe/named-stars/luytens-star.json.cultural: It is named for Willem Jacob Luyten, the astronomer who catalogued the motions of thousands of faint high-velocity stars in the 20th century. Its planet's proximity has made it a focus of both exoplanet study and speculation about contact.

universe/named-stars/menkalinan.json.fact: The 'shoulder of the rein-holder' — a pair of stars that eclipse each other every few days.
universe/named-stars/menkalinan.json.bio: Menkalinan (Beta Aurigae) is a system about 81 light-years away, the second-brightest star in Auriga. Its two nearly identical white stars orbit so closely that they periodically pass in front of one another, dimming the star slightly in a four-day rhythm.
universe/named-stars/menkalinan.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the shoulder of the rein-holder' — the charioteer Auriga, who drives across the northern winter sky with the goat Capella on his shoulder.

universe/named-stars/menkent.json.fact: 'The shoulder of the Centaur' — a nearby orange giant.
universe/named-stars/menkent.json.bio: Menkent (Theta Centauri) is an orange giant about 61 light-years away, one of the brighter stars of Centaurus and the only one of the constellation's leading lights that is a cool giant rather than a hot blue star.
universe/named-stars/menkent.json.cultural: The name means 'the shoulder of the Centaur'. Centaurus, home also to the Sun's nearest neighbours Alpha and Proxima Centauri, is one of the grandest figures of the southern sky.

universe/named-stars/miaplacidus.json.fact: The second light of the Keel — a white star with a curiously blended name.
universe/named-stars/miaplacidus.json.bio: Miaplacidus (Beta Carinae) is a white star about 113 light-years away, the second-brightest in the southern constellation Carina, the Keel of the ancient ship Argo.
universe/named-stars/miaplacidus.json.cultural: Its unusual name appears to fuse an Arabic word for 'waters' with the Latin 'placidus' ('placid'). Deep in the southern sky, it was charted by the navigators and astronomers who mapped the far south.

universe/named-stars/mimosa.json.fact: The second-brightest gem of the Southern Cross, blazing hot blue.
universe/named-stars/mimosa.json.bio: Mimosa (Beta Crucis), also known as Becrux, is a hot blue giant roughly 280 light-years away and one of the hottest bright stars visible to the eye. It pulsates subtly and lies within the striking figure of the Southern Cross.
universe/named-stars/mimosa.json.cultural: As a principal star of Crux, Mimosa shares in the Cross's prominence on southern flags and in southern-hemisphere navigation and myth, from Aboriginal Australian sky-stories to Andean cosmology.

universe/named-stars/mintaka.json.fact: The westernmost star of Orion's Belt — poised almost exactly on the celestial equator.
universe/named-stars/mintaka.json.bio: Mintaka (Delta Orionis) is a hot, massive multiple system more than a thousand light-years away, the western star of Orion's Belt. It lies so close to the celestial equator that it rises very nearly due east and sets very nearly due west for observers everywhere on Earth.
universe/named-stars/mintaka.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the belt'. As one of the three Belt stars, it shares in the near-universal recognition of Orion, and its place on the equator made it a natural marker of east and west.

universe/named-stars/mirfak.json.fact: The luminous heart of Perseus, leading a scattered cluster of young stars.
universe/named-stars/mirfak.json.bio: Mirfak (Alpha Persei) is a yellow-white supergiant roughly 510 light-years away, the brightest star in Perseus. It is the leading light of the Alpha Persei Cluster, a loose group of hot young stars sharing its motion through space.
universe/named-stars/mirfak.json.cultural: The name comes from the Arabic for 'the elbow'. In the classical figure Perseus holds the head of Medusa — near the winking demon-star Algol — and Mirfak marks the hero's side.

universe/named-stars/nunki.json.fact: A hot blue star of the Archer — and one of the very few surviving Babylonian star names.
universe/named-stars/nunki.json.bio: Nunki (Sigma Sagittarii) is a hot blue main-sequence star about 230 light-years away, the second-brightest in Sagittarius. It forms part of the 'Teapot' asterism, near where the Milky Way is richest.
universe/named-stars/nunki.json.cultural: 'Nunki' is one of the rare star names handed down directly from ancient Mesopotamia, recorded by the Babylonians thousands of years ago and preserved through to modern star catalogues.

universe/named-stars/peacock.json.fact: The brightest star of the Peacock — an English name born of 20th-century navigation.
universe/named-stars/peacock.json.bio: Peacock (Alpha Pavonis) is a hot blue system about 180 light-years away, the brightest star in Pavo, the Peacock, deep in the southern sky.
universe/named-stars/peacock.json.cultural: Like Avior, its name is modern: the British nautical almanac of the 1930s required names for bright southern stars, and 'Peacock' was coined from its constellation. Pavo was one of the southern 'bird' constellations of the exploration era.

universe/named-stars/polaris.json.fact: Today's North Star — sitting almost exactly above Earth's north pole, a fixed point around which the sky appears to turn.
universe/named-stars/polaris.json.bio: Polaris (Alpha Ursae Minoris) is a yellow supergiant and a Cepheid variable roughly 430 light-years away. It is not especially bright; its fame comes entirely from its position near the celestial pole.
universe/named-stars/polaris.json.cultural: For navigators across the northern hemisphere, Polaris gives both direction (true north) and latitude (its altitude equals your latitude). Precession means it has not always been, and will not always be, the pole star.

universe/named-stars/pollux.json.fact: The brighter of the Heavenly Twins — an orange giant with a planet of its own.
universe/named-stars/pollux.json.bio: Pollux (Beta Geminorum) is an orange-hued giant star just 34 light-years away, the nearest giant to the Sun. It hosts a confirmed gas-giant planet, Pollux b, discovered from the star's slight wobble.
universe/named-stars/pollux.json.cultural: Pollux and neighbouring Castor are the 'Dioscuri', the twin brothers of Greek and Roman myth — Pollux the immortal son of Zeus. The pair have guided and guarded sailors since antiquity.

universe/named-stars/procyon.json.fact: The 'forerunner of the dog' — it rises just before Sirius to announce the Dog Star.
universe/named-stars/procyon.json.bio: Procyon (Alpha Canis Minoris) is a nearby white main-sequence star only 11.5 light-years away, orbited by a faint white-dwarf companion. Its closeness makes it the eighth-brightest star in the sky despite its modest true luminosity.
universe/named-stars/procyon.json.cultural: The Greek name means 'before the dog', because from many latitudes Procyon climbs above the horizon shortly ahead of Sirius. With Sirius and Betelgeuse it forms the bright 'Winter Triangle'.

universe/named-stars/proxima-centauri.js.fact: The closest star to the Sun — a dim red dwarf just 4.24 light-years away, host to a potentially rocky planet in its habitable zone.
universe/named-stars/proxima-centauri.js.bio: Proxima Centauri is a small, cool red dwarf, the third member of the Alpha Centauri system. It is far too faint to see with the naked eye despite its proximity, and it flares violently — a challenge for any planet's habitability.
universe/named-stars/proxima-centauri.js.cultural: As our nearest stellar neighbour, Proxima is the natural first target for interstellar thought experiments, from Breakthrough Starshot's light-sail probes to generations of science fiction.

universe/named-stars/rasalhague.json.fact: The 'head of the serpent-bearer' — the crown of the healer who holds the snake.
universe/named-stars/rasalhague.json.bio: Rasalhague (Alpha Ophiuchi) is a white star about 48 light-years away, the brightest in Ophiuchus, the Serpent-Bearer. It spins rapidly and is orbited by a low-mass companion.
universe/named-stars/rasalhague.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the head of the serpent-collector'. Ophiuchus — often identified with the healer Asclepius grasping a great snake — straddles the ecliptic, the thirteenth figure the Sun passes through.

universe/named-stars/regulus.json.fact: The 'little king' at the heart of the Lion — a flattened, fast-spinning royal star on the ecliptic.
universe/named-stars/regulus.json.bio: Regulus (Alpha Leonis) is a hot blue-white star about 79 light-years away, the brightest in Leo. It whirls so rapidly that it is visibly flattened, and it heads a multiple system with fainter companions. Lying almost exactly on the ecliptic, it is regularly passed — and occasionally occulted — by the Moon and planets.
universe/named-stars/regulus.json.cultural: Named 'little king' by Copernicus and known anciently as the Lion's Heart (Cor Leonis), Regulus was one of the four 'Royal Stars' of Persia that marked the turning of the seasons.

universe/named-stars/rigel.json.fact: A brilliant blue supergiant — the luminous foot of Orion, tens of thousands of times brighter than the Sun.
universe/named-stars/rigel.json.bio: Rigel (Beta Orionis) is a hot blue supergiant several hundred light-years away, one of the most intrinsically luminous stars visible to the naked eye. Despite the 'Beta' designation it usually outshines Betelgeuse.
universe/named-stars/rigel.json.cultural: The name comes from the Arabic for 'foot'. Rigel's steely blue-white light is a classic contrast to Betelgeuse's red across the figure of Orion.

universe/named-stars/rigil-kentaurus.jso.fact: The Sun's nearest bright neighbour — a golden twin of the Sun anchoring the front foot of the Centaur.
universe/named-stars/rigil-kentaurus.jso.bio: Rigil Kentaurus (Alpha Centauri A) is the brightest member of the closest stellar system to the Sun, just 4.3 light-years away. A near-twin of the Sun in colour and mass, it forms a bright binary with the cooler Alpha Centauri B, while the faint red dwarf Proxima Centauri orbits far out as the actual nearest star.
universe/named-stars/rigil-kentaurus.jso.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'foot of the Centaur'. Together with nearby Hadar it forms the 'Pointers' that guide southern observers to the Southern Cross, and as the closest Sun-like star it is a perennial target of interstellar-travel studies and fiction.

universe/named-stars/sadr.json.fact: The breast of the Swan — a luminous supergiant at the heart of the Northern Cross, wrapped in glowing gas.
universe/named-stars/sadr.json.bio: Sadr (Gamma Cygni) is a yellow-white supergiant roughly 1,800 light-years away, sitting at the intersection of the Northern Cross where the wings of Cygnus meet the body. It is embedded against a vast complex of glowing hydrogen known as the Sadr region.
universe/named-stars/sadr.json.cultural: The name is Arabic for 'the chest' or 'breast'. As the centre of the Northern Cross, Sadr rides the brightest reach of the summer Milky Way, in the direction of one of its richest star clouds.

universe/named-stars/saiph.json.fact: A blue supergiant at Orion's knee — Rigel's hotter, fainter-looking twin.
universe/named-stars/saiph.json.bio: Saiph (Kappa Orionis) is a blue supergiant roughly 650 light-years away, marking the lower-left corner of Orion opposite Rigel. It is comparable to Rigel in size and heat, but appears fainter to us because much of its fierce output pours out as invisible ultraviolet light.
universe/named-stars/saiph.json.cultural: The name comes from the Arabic for 'sword'. Saiph and Rigel are the two 'feet' of the Hunter, framing the base of one of the most recognisable figures in the sky.

universe/named-stars/sargas.json.fact: A bright giant in the Scorpion's raised tail, carrying an ancient Mesopotamian name.
universe/named-stars/sargas.json.bio: Sargas (Theta Scorpii) is a yellow-white bright giant roughly 300 light-years away, one of the leading stars in the curving tail of Scorpius near its stinger.
universe/named-stars/sargas.json.cultural: The name appears to be of Sumerian or Babylonian origin, a rare survival from Mesopotamian star-lore. In the sky it lies along the Scorpion's tail as it sweeps through the bright clouds of the southern Milky Way.

universe/named-stars/sirius.json.fact: The brightest star in Earth's night sky — and one of our nearest stellar neighbours at 8.6 light-years.
universe/named-stars/sirius.json.bio: Sirius (Alpha Canis Majoris) is a hot, blue-white main-sequence star with a faint white-dwarf companion, Sirius B, the burnt-out core of a once more-massive star. Its brilliance comes from a genuinely luminous star sitting unusually close to us.
universe/named-stars/sirius.json.cultural: The 'Dog Star' has guided calendars for millennia: its heliacal rising once heralded the annual flooding of the Nile in ancient Egypt, and it anchors the 'Dog Days' of summer in the Greco-Roman tradition.

universe/named-stars/spica.json.fact: The 'ear of wheat' in the Maiden's hand — a close pair whose dance helped reveal precession.
universe/named-stars/spica.json.bio: Spica (Alpha Virginis) is a hot blue pair of stars about 250 light-years away, so close together that they orbit in just four days and are distorted into egg shapes by mutual gravity. Their combined light makes Spica the brightest star in Virgo.
universe/named-stars/spica.json.cultural: Its Latin name means 'ear of grain', the sheaf of wheat held by Virgo the harvest maiden. Observations of Spica let Hipparchus detect the slow precession of the equinoxes over two thousand years ago.

universe/named-stars/van-maanens-star.js.fact: The nearest lone white dwarf — the burnt-out, Earth-sized ember of a dead star.
universe/named-stars/van-maanens-star.js.bio: Van Maanen's Star is a white dwarf about 14 light-years away in Pisces, the closest solitary white dwarf to the Sun. Once a Sun-like star, it has exhausted its fuel and collapsed to roughly the size of Earth, now slowly cooling as a dense stellar cinder.
universe/named-stars/van-maanens-star.js.cultural: It is named for Adriaan van Maanen, who discovered it in 1917. Its spectrum shows heavy elements that betray rocky debris raining onto it — early evidence that planetary systems can outlive their stars.

universe/named-stars/vega.json.fact: The brightest star of Lyra, and once — and future — Pole Star as Earth's axis slowly precesses.
universe/named-stars/vega.json.bio: Vega (Alpha Lyrae) is a nearby hot white star, only 25 light-years away, that long served as the zero-point reference for the astronomical magnitude scale. It rotates so fast it is noticeably flattened.
universe/named-stars/vega.json.cultural: Vega was the northern pole star around 12,000 BCE and will be again near 13,700 CE. It anchors the Summer Triangle with Deneb and Altair, and stars in Carl Sagan's Contact as the source of the alien signal.

universe/named-stars/wezen.json.fact: A supergiant of the Great Dog, so luminous it shines brightly from far across the galaxy.
universe/named-stars/wezen.json.bio: Wezen (Delta Canis Majoris) is a yellow-white supergiant around 1,600 light-years away. To appear as bright as it does from that distance, it must pour out tens of thousands of times the Sun's light — a star nearing the end of its life.
universe/named-stars/wezen.json.cultural: The name comes from an Arabic word for 'weight'. It lies in Canis Major, the Great Dog that follows Orion across the sky behind brilliant Sirius.
